Mr. Speaker, this question has been, standing for a long time. It was amended. The answer to the first section, as nearly as we can secure the information is -1,060.
The second, third and fourth questions are ambiguously framed. The answer I think would be "yes," were it not for the fact that the words "or support such request", are used, which might perhaps leave a wrong impression on the minds of 'hon. members. The letter to which the hon. gentleman refers is dated November 18, 1930, and is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. It was signed by Messrs. Bracken, Anderson and Brownlee; so all three supported the suggestions. The letter made four suggestions, and I will read them so they may appear as part of the answer:
1.	That, without in any way interfering with the free movement or sale of wheat by grain companies and exporting agencies, the producers of wheat be assured of a domestic price of not less than 70 cents Fort William. This suggestion is based on the fact that producers of wheat to-day are passing through world conditions not of their making and that they should not be singled out as one industry that must work through these conditions unassisted by the state.
2.	Failing this, that the dominion government, by guarantee or otherwise, assure the banks against loss in carrying on the wheat pool in an orderly way under such direction as they care to arrange to satisfy themselves that marketing is being properly carried out. This suggestion is based on the conviction that uncertainty as to the pool's financial position may be the most disturbing factor to-day. We also point out that the present initial payment was arranged with all the accumulated knowledge in Canada at the time as to world's con-

ditions and in the belief that it was a safe payment.
3.	Failing either of these, that the government establish a stabilization board with financial support to purchase wheat whenever the market falls below certain minimum levels. It is respectfully submitted that at present levels this action would involve a minimum of or no loss and would not be accompanied by any of the dangers which surrounded the American wheat board when it first began operation with wheat at more than double present prices.
4.	Aside from the above, we suggested your government might consider the advisability of instructing the Board of Grain Commissioners to inquire into short selling on the Winnipeg grain exchange with a view to proper action against offenders.

speechtext:
Motions 51 and 52, I submit, should not 'be passed by the house, for the reasons which I submitted the other day. They contemplate the production by the railway company of correspondence which it has had with a citizen of the country who is not a member of this house. It is alleged, as a matter of fact, that part of a letter was published in a newspaper. That cannot in any sense affect the principle involved, the application of which, I submit, precludes this house from passing these motions which stand in the name of the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot).. It is quite wrong to expect the government to ask the railway companies to provide copies of letters that may be written to them by citizens of the country with respect to the construction of stations or other works. If that were done, we should be engaged most of the time in the production of such correspondence, inasmuch as the communities affected are writing letters continuously to the railway officials with respect to matters of this kind, And the fact that someone who writes a letter happens to have been an opponent of an hon. member of this house cannot assist the hon. gentleman's case. Nor can the fact that that same citizen used a portion of his letter in a communication addressed to a newspaper advance the matter further. I therefore say to my hon. friend that reluctantly we are compelled to deny him this source of information, though I have no

In regard to the question raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) as to the necessity of following the procedure with regard to government notices of motion, I direct the attention of the house to standing order 60 which reads as follows:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the con-
sideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
That standing order is in keeping word for word with the British standing order No. 71, passed on March 20, 1866.

A notice of motion has to be given and before the motion can be considered notice must be given that the committee will be set up. I gave notice the other day that I would make a formal motion to-morrow, and it is under that rule I took the exception which I did. The action which I took is covered by that rule.

The Speaker is in the
hands of the house and acting as he has today he has been following precedent. It may not be a correct interpretation of the rule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Your Honour will observe that the rule says that the house cannot at once consider the matter. Under the heading of government notices of motion I gave notice that I would to-morrow or at the next sitting of the house move that the house resolve itself into a committee to consider the motion standing under my name. Now, what could anyone second; it is not a question of seconding that motion, there can only be a seconder to a motion and there is no motion. The motion will come to-morrow or at the next sitting when I move that the Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into a committee of the whole to consider the resolution.

Then, under that interpretation of this rule, when the motion is made to-morrow or at whatever sitting of the house it may be made, it cannot be dealt with but will have to be adjourned. I repeat the rule as follows:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
If the motion to refer the matter to committee of the whole is not put and carried, then, when it comes on for consideration tomorrow, it cannot be dealt with, but will have to be adjourned again.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, up until this morning I had intended to allocate my precious forty minutes as follows:
Eight or ten minutes, or maybe six or eight minutes to my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), because I am sure that the minister must feel that my comments are long overdue.
Eight or ten minutes was to be allocated to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) in connection with his remarks on the budget, and the balance of my time was to

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
be allocated to the budget itself. However, when I surveyed my ammunition I came to the conclusion that I could not possibly fire it all in forty minutes, so I am obliged reluctantly to pass up the Minister of Agriculture until a more convenient season, possibly on his estimates, and proceed at once to the budget and my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a doughty warrior and an able debater and I expected that he would have taken up the cudgels in defence of the remarkable action taken by his leader while at the London conference. It will be remembered that there was a ministerial quartette over there, two members of which have spoken but neither has referred to the belligerent conduct of their leader. That action was very flamboyant and similar to what would be expected from Big Bill Thompson of Chicago or Jack Dempsey; it was of a Donnvbrook nature all round. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) shied away from any mention of that action, although he did refer very modestly to the conference by telling us how he had allayed the feeling that Canada was holding up her wheat and possibly prices in relation to Great Britain. It is generally good generalship to attack, whether in the field of battle or on the platform, provided one has anything to attack about, but if one attacks without justification there is generally a backfire, and that is what's about to happen in this case.
My hon. friend asked quite grandiloquently and somewhat challengingly: What did the Minister of Agriculture do when he came back from Europe in 1928 in order to fix up things and allay the difficulty which he complained of? What did Hon. Mr. Dunning, then Minister of Railways, a supposed authority on wheat matters, do when he came back? What did the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart) do? The hon. minister left the impression that we had been sitting around doing nothing in particular.
In the autumn of 1929, after the stock market crash, the first evidence appeared that there was something like a tendency towards too much wheat in the world. During that time I could not find a single authority on the wheat situation who would admit that we had anything like too much wheat or that prices were likely to drop. The pool men also, Jim Richardson and Jim Stewart, would not admit that, and I could not find one single authority who did not think it quite safe to hold wheat stocks for higher prices. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce,
with his back sight now thinks that something should have been done by the government of that day.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was looking at the hon. member.	-

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF THE DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am quite willing to take up that near-challenge, although I do not hope to deal with it as thoroughly as I would if I had unlimited time. I went over to Europe in 1928 to see for myself what truth there was in the allegations that our wheat was being deteriorated by the practice of wheat mixing later abolished by the King government, which became so extensive during 1925, 1926 and 1927. I visited every important market, in continental Europe and Great Britain including London, Liverpool, Edinburgh, Belfast, Dublin, Hamburg, Rotterdam, Amsterdam, Antwerp, Brussels and Paris. In every case except the last I found very grave complaints with respect to the deteriorated quality of our wheat. Sitting around the board of the Liverpool com exchange, of which Mr. Urquhart was the secretary, there were some eighteen members of the council. The Hon. Mr. Hamilton of Regina was with me and we sat and talked there for over an hour. We found great indignation at the low quality of our wheat and because of the fact that this condition occurred practically simultaneously with the organization of the pools in the west, they were disposed to blame the pools for the mixing. I remember one very indignant gentleman asked whether we actually sprayed water into the wheat in order to make it absorb more moisture up to the maximum percentage allowed and thus weigh more. The first complaint was in regard to the mixing and deterioration of our wheat seriously below the old standard; the other was that the pool that had suddenly sprung upon the scene had something to do with the matter because as already stated the organization of the pool and the mixing and deterioration occurred about the same time. I tried to smooth things over and I succeeded with them all except two who were badly bitten importers that nothing would satisfy. After visiting other places where I had practically identical experiences, I returned home. I arrived in Regina, as it happened, on the occasion of a luncheon given by the pool in honour of representatives of the weekly newspapers then assembled in that city. On that occasion I was asked to address the luncheoners and I explained overseas wheat conditions as I am doing now. I told the pool they had many friends in the old country and in continental Europe, but naturally they had some enemies. No organization like that could spring into exist-

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
enee so suddenly, powerfully and spectacularly without creating some enemies. As a matter of fact, they made some enemies on whose toes they had. trampled because they were wanting to sell as directly as possible to the consumer. But I informed them that they had more friends than enemies and that they should rigidly maintain the quality of our wheat. Living so far from both oceans, I suggested it was imperative that we should have the very best wheat exports if we were to be on an equal footing with our competitors all over the world.
Why should we have interfered in 1929? My hon. friend did not say what we should have done. He was very careful as to that; he did not say that we should have taken charge of the wheat as the government foolishly did, I think in 1917 it was. We all recall how the government commandeered the wheat at Fort William, and no one yet knows why. He did not even suggest that. Why should we have done anything drastic in 1929 with the prices then prevailing? These are the official figures which I obtained just this morning for 1927, 1928, 1929, 1930 and 1931 for wheat. After I have given them, we might well ask ourselves why any government should have interfered, as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce suggests we should have done, in the fall of 1929:

When my hon. friends took charge of government on August 7 last, No. 1 northern wheat basis Fort William was $1; now it is 58} cents and was down as low as 50 cents. What are the government fussing about now when they did not do anything themselves when wheat was at 58} cents at Fort William although they wanted the Liberals to do something drastic when it was from $1.39 to $1.41 in October, November and December, 1929, or over twice as much?
After the freight is deducted, the value of the wheat to the farmer on the first of June, 1930, or just about the time parliament prorogued, was 93} cents at the average shipping point, say in Saskatchewan. On the first of June, 1931, the value was 43} cents net to farmer or 53 cents less this year under a Tory government than it was last year under a Liberal administration. The inference on my hon. friend's part was that the Liberal administration was responsible and 
that we should have done something. I wonder if my hon. friends would want to do anything drastic to-day about wheat if it stood at $1.11} on June 1. I believe they would think they were in clover under such good prices. On the 7th August last year when my hon. friends came into power, I repeat, wheat was at $1 a bushel at Fort William on the basis of No. 1 northern. Today it is hovering around sixty cents and it has been down to fifty cents. There was apparently some attempt on the government's part to do something, through Hon. H. Ferguson in London, but they did not do anything. What were these gentleman going to do now who in 1929 were going to round up the world in regard to wheat? When there was a suggestion of a conference with Russia, our friend the High Commissioner for Canada in London must needs go to Rome and attend the International Institute of Agriculture there where an international wheat conference was being held at the same time. Before he was there twenty-four hours, he had them all at each other's ears, divided into two hostile camps; the exporters and the importers. The result was that he, the high commissioner, went to London with the exporters and left the remaining ones the importers to organize and go to Paris as a rival organization. These are two great diplomatic Canadians:	the
Prime Minister and his appointee in London. They are two choice diplomats, two of the same kind. They go out with bludgeons, upset the whole applecart and their merchandizing efforts are naturally abortive. The London conference was abortive; they did not do anything except appoint a continuing committee to gather statistics that were already being collected by the Agricultural Institute at Rome and the League of Nations.
But they did finally do something. Yes, there was the five cent bonus to absorb some freight on export wheat. We on this side have been chastised for not having approved of this five cent absorption. We are not sure just who is going to be benefited. We are of opinion it is intended by the Prime Minister to be in the nature of compensation for what we have had to pay for the high protection imposed on our goods last year, in the September session and again this year. The increase from 6 to 7} per cent imposed by the previous government on our farm implements has been raised to 25 per cent by this government. Even if we get this five cents per bushel bonus, it is something that is coming to the farmers and we are prepared to take that little crumb from the rich government's table provided it is a crumb, provided it is a little bit

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
of bread instead of a stone, provided it is fish instead of a serpent. We are not yet sure what it k. Under the law as it exists and as announced by the Prime Minister, the only one who can earn that five cents is the exporter. I say that without any reservation. How is one to know what is being exported except from the documents which the exporter holds. If that be so-and it is so-the farmers will not get that five cent3. How will it be known where the wheat is going? How will the farmer know? How will the initial buyer know? A great many of the domestic millers buy their wheat straight from Fort William, not knowing or caring who grew it originally or where it came from. Consequently the conclusion we arrive at as the proposal now stands, and it is a logical conclusion, is that the exporter is the only one that can earn this five cents, and he may split it with the buyer abroad in order to ensure a sale in this depressed market. That means that the miller on the other side of the water will be subsidized by Canada against the Canadian milling interests. And that policy comes from the Canada first party! Surely that was not their intention but that is apparently the policy that was announced by the Prime Minister in his budget. I am as satisfied as that I am standing here that the only way that policy can be carried out in accordance with what seemed to be the intent of the Prime Minister is to give the five cents to the farmer at the point of shipment, and give it on all wheat. You cannot make a distinction between export wheat and domestic wheat. It is utterly impossible.
There is one way in which this policy might be worked out. Under the old wheat board the farmers got participation certificates. Every farmer who sold a load or carload of wheat in 1919 received an advance of $2.15 a bushel for No. 1 at Fort William, and for the balance he received a participation certificate, which he presented to the wheat board after the year's operations were over, and then got his final payment. The same might be done in the case of the five cent freight bonus. Give the farmer that ships a load of wheat either for domestic or export use a participation freight certificate for five cents, per bushel and then present that to the government foi payment. That is I believe the only way to do it. I am giving the government a tip on this matter, and while I am giving advice and pointing out how the policy might be worked out, I would say that it is absurd to discriminate against coarse grains, because when you limit it to wheat you are subsidizing the one thing that should not be subsidized. But
the government are offering this as a peace offering to the west, and in limiting the policy to wheat they are discriminating against the man who finds it more convenient to grow rye, or barley or some other grain Our friends here from the west know that there are some farming districts that are not suitable for growing wheat, and the government is going to penalize them by not giving them this crumb, if it proves to be a crumb. It is an attempt to speed up the one thing we do not want to speed up artificially, and that is the acreage of wheat. I do not think it will be speeded up much by this policy, if at all, but certainly the policy discriminates against the man who is growing coarse grains and feeding stock in districts where wheat cannot be grown to advantage. So I would make the further suggestion that the government, instead of making two bites at a cherry and mumbling around all about it and trying to do something for the farmer that they do not know how to do apparently, should come straight out with the bonus for all cereals, and then there will be no difficulty in the clerical work associated with such a workable policy. I know the government will not take this advice. They do not know even that it is good advice. They are just blundering along, hopelessly helpless and helplessly hopeless, in their vain attempts to do something.

None knows that
better than the Tory rearguard over there. I have some further figures, Mr. Speaker. I wish I could make the clock stand still like Joshua did the sun, but time is passing. So much for my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. Unless this five cent policy is rescued at once it will do more harm instead of good to the farmers. It will be simply subsidizing the dumping of wheat on markets that are already over-dumped. Like my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, who, when he thought a month or so ago that butter had reached a "rock bottom" price at 22 cents a pound, agreed with the Australian authorities that they could dump vast quantities of Australian butter in Vancouver on the market, only to find then a still lower "rock botom." That is what they are apparently going to do now with the five cent speech-the five cent bonus to the wheat exporters unless quickly switched in committee to the western farmers.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Yes, it is another
five cent speech, with very much more in

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
it than the other one. The farmers in the west know that this five cent policy as it stands now is not worth anything, and they are as mad as wet hens over it. It is just pretending to do something. Where did the government get the idea to begin with? We have all heard of Robert Whiteside. He thinks that there is a credit balance of nearly $80,000,000 due to the farmers of the west from this government, and he got up on his hind legs and said:	I do not want a pegged
price for wheat so long as the government pays us that money that is owing, by absorbing the freight at the rate of four or five cents a bushel. The government have borrowed the idea from this farmer, it would seem, because he was the first one who announced it, so far as I know. The government however does not know how to put it' into operation. We will have to get Robert Whiteside of Saskatchewan down here.

speechtext: He is here.

speechtext:
I think he is. I
shall be glad to arrange an interview, so that he may advise the government on this freight rate question.
I pass on. I have a note here, "R. B. in London, Paris and Belfast." R. B. is not present. I have never been fortunate enough to have him present this year while I was speaking in the house. I thought I was going to have the Prime Minister honour me by being present to-day, but I am not going to let his absenece prevent me from saying what I have to say. I am going to refer once more, and for the third time, to his remarkable speech at a banquet in Belfast when he was being honoured by one of the greatest seats of learning in the world, in one of the greatest industrial cities in the world, by the university of Belfast. Canada's Prime Minister was worthy of the honour, but what a strange conception he had of gratitude in the speech that he made on that occasion. I have quoted long portions of that speech before, and it has never been noticed by anybody opposite. I felt rather disappointed at this. I thought I had a real scoop, but I was advised never to mind about quotations the next time, but just give it off the bat, and that is what I am going to do.
You can imagine the Belfast hosts all seated around the banqueting table after the decorations had been bestowed on the Prime Minister. The banquet was presided over by Viscount Craigavon, the Ulster premier, a very distinguished gentleman, and among the guests present were the members of the upper house, the lower house, and the judiciary- all the gentry and upper ten of Belfast, and
{Mr. Motherwell.]
there are many there. If you ever want to see a real Irish gentleman, go to Belfast, and they know a gentleman, too, when they see one. When the banqueting was over and the speeches began, our Prime Minister, of course, took a prominent part, among the others, as he always does. It was "a" part though, not "the" part most Canadians would have preferred. On this occasion he led off by telling them that the time had come when the various units of the British commonwealth must be held together by economic ties, and if these economic ties were not provided and gotten from some source, then the British Empire, like other great empires of the past, would dwindle and disappear. I have on another occasion read that portion of his speech, and anybody who wants to challenge me to produce the evidence may be sure that I have not left it upstairs in my room. I have it ready here. But our Prime Minister, not satisfied with that, poked his finger in his hosts' eyes by reminding them of the Boston tea party. Well, every historian and Britisher over there is sorry that the Boston tea party ever happened. It led eventually to the war of independence and to the actual independence of the United States. Who was responsible for that? We know who it was. It was a stupid crown, supported by a feeble minister like Lord North, and they drove the American colonies into independence and where they are to-day. It was this that the Prime Minister reminded his hosts of on the day that they had honoured him. That seems to be the essence of stupidity, if not worse. He went on and repeated it several times; I have the report of his speech here. He said that while at one time the ties of kinship were all right, to-day the world has come to such a pass that there was nothing but the ties of business and economics that would keep the empire together. That kind of jarred our friends in Belfast. They did not say anything about it for a week or two, waiting to hear what Premier Scullin and Premier Forbes of Australia and New Zealand would say on this important question when they arrived in Belfast shortly afterwards. They took absolutely the opposite stand; they said, "All right, let us have ties of an economic nature. But the ties that have held us together so long are the ties of kinship, the ties of blood and tradition, and the chances are that when these go our economic ties will not hold us." After the arrival of Premier Scullin and Premier Forbes, the same newspaper got its second wind, it came to itself, for it had been completely knocked out by the Canadian Prime Minister. They spoke pretty frankly. However, if you want to know

The Budget-Mr. Motherwell
all the rest of it, is it not written in the chronicles of Hansard? To save time I will refer hon. members to my speech in the debate on the address. On this point let me ask: What right has the Prime Minister to castigate the farmers on the prairies, who are in despair and do not know which way to turn, for talking about secession, not knowing what else to talk about to draw attention to their present plight, when he himself, in Belfast of all places on earth, predicts the downfall of the British Empire? No farmer on the prairies ever uttered such a libellous statement against the loyality of the various units of the British commonwealth of nations. And this from the sublime and superloyal Tory party of Canada! Have they become so entirely absorbed in their "Canada first" policy that they are forgetting all else, as if any nation can live to itself? No wonder their policies are what they are. When they want more revenue they shut it off by the imposition of prohibitive tariffs. When they want our dairymen to get a better price for butter they dump Australian butter on our markets. God knows what they will do next! That is what the people are wondering-what will this rattlebrained government do next? I do not know; that is a conundrum. And they do not know themselves, unfortunately.
Now, let me deal with the income tax. We have been castigated for calling this a millionaire's budget. Yes, we have been wrong in that respect-it is a multimillionaire's budget. A lot of the millionaires, the low down fellows on the schedule are taxed higher; it is the multi-millionaires who have gotten away with the swag. This is no guess work. Anyone can get this information where I obtained it-at the taxation office. I should like to put all these figures on Hansard. If they are proud of their budget they should allow me to do so, without reading the whole ghastly record. The small salaried men from $3,000 to S8,000 get a drop in the aggregate of $50 or $60; then those in receipt of taxable incomes, from $9,000 all the way up through the various gradations to $130,000 will have to pay a higher tax.

past the $130/100 into the million dollar taxable income class, those multi-millionaires
in receipt of such incomes are taken care of by this millionaire government. Well, what is the use of being in power if one cannot look after number one and one's multi-millionaire friends? So we have those modest hon. gentlemen sitting around the council table planning how they can relieve the treasury of millions of dollars formerly paid to the treasury under the Robb and Dunning budget. The man in this schedule in receipt of $140,000 of taxable income saves $163, but the rate is graded rapidly until the man with a taxable income of $1,000,000 holds back from the treasury $116,803 that otherwise, I repeat, under the Robb and Dunning budgets would have been paid into the national exchequer.

If I thought it
really was a question, I would permit it even out of my own time. The highest income tax paid or to be paid by the multi-millionaire now by this budget is $246,125. Even under this reduction this income tax is still higher than it is in the United States on similar income taxpayers by about $5,000. How can our friends opposite say, then, that this reduction in the multi-millionaire income tax will attract capital into Canada when our income tax on these very large incomes is still higher than it is in the United States? They cannot have it both ways. I just want-to puncture that little argument, and at the same time incidentally show that the taxation in Canada, is still higher on the multimillionaire than in the United States. Therefore the government cannot claim any justification for the expectation that this

budget will attract capital back to Canada because of this adjustment of the income tax.
But as bad as this is, there is worse to come. Just think of it, Mr. Speaker; here we have a government which admittedly includes at least four millionaires, possibly multimillionaires, sitting around the council table and trying their best to withhold millions of dollars from the treasury by lowering the income tax on multimillionaires. Why, Mr. Speaker, if I bought a jimmy and a kit of safe-cracking utensils and started out to do the same thing on the treasury bank, I would be in the penitentiary in no time, but because one can do it legally, around the council table, it is a different thing.

speechtext:
What is not true?
I have before me, Mr. Speaker, a copy of the old War Revenue Act of 1929. This budget is much worse, as under it, the exemptions under the sales tax have been shot to pieces.

The Budget-Mr. Mullins
Under the Dunning budget there was a very-exhaustive list of sales tax exemptions, but these all have been cancelled and a new, but much smaller schedule, substituted. I defy anyone to state definitely what sales tax exemptions have been changed or dropped without most laborious research. It is all mixed up; it is not in the same consecutive order, and no layman can work it out correctly. I have done the best I could, and I find a number of articles which were exempted from sales tax in former budgets which do not carry that exemption now. For instance there is condensed milk, evaporated milk and powdered milk; lard compound and similar substances, made from animal or vegetable stear-ine or oils; hops; chicory, raw or green; materials for use only in the construction, equipment and repair of ships; ships licensed to engage in the Canadian coasting trade; manila fibre for use only in the manufacture of rope not exceeding one and one-half inches in circumference for the fisheries and boats bona fide purchased by individual fishermen for their own personal use in the fisheries.
I have only about four minutes; I do not know whether I shall be allowed the time taken up in interruptions, so I will not continue, although there are 135 formerly exempted tariff items with which I have not time to deal. However, before these items are taken up in committee I hope the government will bring down something more specific as to the changes which have been made with respect to these articles which were exempt under the old Sales tax, but which are not now exempt. I think there are scores if not fifties of those items; there are so many that at short notice one cannot find them all.
Is there not something with a heart the government can do? Cannot some good come out of Nazareth? Have this government done nothing good? Yes, they have; what about [DOT] the Stamp commission, and a good commission, which found out what we already knew through the Turgeon commission? The government found out what they should have known; they found what everyone else knew, and what the Turgeon commission reported some years ago, that future selling was unavoidable. Why, all kinds of commodities are bought for future delivery; even transportation, especially water transportation, is bought for future delivery right in the city of Ottawa, yet these precious hon. gentlemen, composing this alleged business-like government, had to ask a commission to find out what was so obvious to everyone and which was before them in the report of the Turgeon commission presented to the government of five or six years
ago. Speaking of the Stamp commission reminds me of postage stamps and Bennett budgets, as-
Every time we lick a stamp,
Or drink a cup of tea,
And see our scanty coin recede We'll swear at the great R.B.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to my hon. friend and neighbour, I cannot help thinking he is like a bird which is described in the dictionary. It is called the dodo bird, and it flies backward but does not know where it is going. It does not look where it is going; it just looks in the direction from which it came. I never heard a better country school campaign talk than that just delivered by the hon. member opposite. He talked about wheat, as usual, nothing but wheat, and he went over to England to do something. I should like to know what he did. He toured all over England in a high powered car with a chauffeur, but what did agriculture get? It got nothing.
I have only a limited time to speak, so I must hurry on. When I think of the great men of Canadian politics of the olden days, I wonder what they would think of the speech of my right hon. friend if they were looking down and listening to him. As a contrast let me read what Hon. George Brown said in Belleville in 1857:
Who cannot see that Providence has entrusted to us the building up of a great northern people fit to cope with our neighbours of the United States and to advance step by step with them in the march of civilization? Sir, it is my fervent aspiration and belief that some here to-night may live to see the day when the British flag shall proudly wave from Labrador to Vancouver island, and from our own Niagara to the shores of Hudson bay. Look abroad over the world and tell me what country possesses the advantages, if she but uses them aright, for achieving such a future as Canada enjoys.
And now listen to what Sir John A. Macdonald said. I should like the ex-Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) to listen, because I have a message for him. He has a habit, when hon. members on this side are speaking, of finding fault or not paying attention; he read a newspaper upside down the last time I spoke in the house, so I ask him now to pay attention to what I am going to say. We are neighbours in western Canada, and I should like him to carry to that country the message I am going to give him. I want him to listen to what Sir John A. Macdonald said:
When this union takes place we will be at the outset no inconsiderable people. We find ourselves with a population approaching four
The Budget-Mr. Mullins

millions of souls. Such a population in Europe would make a second or at least a third rate power, and with a rapidly increasing population, for I am satisfied that under this union our population will increase in a still greater ratio then ever before-with increased credit -with a higher position in the eyes of Europe -with the increased security we can offer to immigrants, "who would naturally prefer to seek a new home in what is known to them as a great country, than in any one little colony or another-with all this I am satisfied that, great as has been our increase in the last twenty-five years since the union between upper and lower Canada, our future progress, during the next quarter of a century, will be vastly greater. And when, by means of this rapid increase, we become a nation of eight or nine millions of inhabitants, our alliance will be worthy of being sought by the great nations of the earth .... Instead of looking upon us as a merely dependent colony, England "will have in us a friendly nation-a subordinate but still a powerful people-to stand by her in North America in peace or in war.
Then I come to what Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
We have learned to love British institutions, because in British institutions we have found more freedom than we could have had as subjects of France. How many times in that grand old city (Quebec), which I have the honour to represent, looking at the banner of St George waving over her proud citadel; How many times have I said to myself that that flag represented the defeat of my ancestors, but at the same time recalled the thought that it was the flag, the most precious to the human race, the flag" of liberty. I love England. I honour and esteem English institutions. I do not regret that we are now subjects of the queen instead of France; but may my right hand wither at my side if the memories of my forefathers ever cease to be dear to my heart.
These great men walked the streets of Ottawa but a few short years ago. I wonder what they would think, listening to such speeches, such wailings as we have heard from the other side. It was said, and rightly, what doubting Thomases! Do they remember when in 1927 the Conservative party voted with them? The gentleman who defeated me took fright and said, there must be something wrong when the Conservatives will vote with the Liberals; there is something wrong with the budget.
Now, there is no narrow, small politics on this side; we are too big for that. We have never played narrow, small, picayune politics. We are here for greater things. We want to build up this dominion, and we cannot do so if we indulge in that sort of thing.
I wish now to say a few words with respect to the tariff. The hon. gentleman said that we went all over the country talking on every platform nothing but butter, and that we slipped in on Australian butter. That is absolutely wrong. We used the tariff on every platform; we used the Dunning 'budget on every
I Mr. Mullins.]
platform. And we did use the butter. I admit it. But we were justified in using it. Any minister of agriculture or any government who would make a treaty like that, against the interests of the dairy industry of this country, had a right to be defeated. Hon. gentlemen opposite have a right to sit where they are now, and I am afraid it will be a long time before they reach this side again.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have preached free trade and practised protection. When was there ever a greater protectionist budget than the Dunning budget, with its countervailing duties. I have here a cartoon; I wonder whether the ex-Minister of Agriculture ever saw it. It certainly went a long way towards the defeat of hon. gentlemen opposite. It shows the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) swimming, and along comes Mr. Dunning and steals every bit of his clothing; he steals the protective principle and the protective policy of the right hon. gentleman. I will let the ex-Minister of Agriculture see the cartoon if he wishes; it appeared in the Country Guide, which surely is not a Conservative paper. As I say, that cartoon had much to do with the defeat of the party opposite. Stealing the policy of those on this side of the house-do they call that fair politics? They steal every item of our policy, preaching free trade and practising protection.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you cannot have a prosperous country without protection, and I am not afraid to talk protection if I do come from a constituency which has not a smokestack in its entire area. My constituency is all agriculture, but I want to tell hon. gentlemen opposite that we do not care a snap of the finger for duties: the tariff is not bothering us at all. Let me assure my hon. friends that they can no longer preach free trade and win a seat with that doctrine. But what does it matter what the tariff is so long as we can buy goods at the right prices? [DOT] I remember buying a binder for $150 when the tariff was 33J per cent. I see the exMinister of Agriculture is going out; I am sorry, because I have a lot of material which I was going to give him later on. He knows that I am coming to the live stock end of the discussion. No, Mr. Speaker; you cannot preach free trade any longer because the farmers will not accept it. As I was saying,
I could buy a binder for $150 when the duty was 33 i per cent. But, I repeat, what difference does it make what the duty is so long as the consumer is not exploited?
The Prime Minister has told the country that he will not permit the consumer to be exploited. If that is the case, surely my free

The Budget-Mr. Mullins
trade friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young) can want no more. There is a lot of fault found about increases in various lines, but I take a clipping from a newspaper and I find that commodities have not been raised in price. Machinery has not gone up in price, the prices of staple commodities have not gone up, and the fact is that a high tariff does not mean a raising of prices.
Does my hon. friend refer only to commodities produced at home, or does he refer to importations alone? He says the tariff has not raised prices.
It does not raise the price of any commodity.
Hard coal has gone up.
No, it has not.
Yes, it has in my town.
It is $1.10 cheaper than it was last year.
Not in Ontario.
Read the paper.

I know what it is in my
own town.

I have here a document drawn up by the manufacturers under their own signature, in which they agree not to raise the prices. In many cases they have reduced them. There is the document, under* taking that prices shall not be advanced. As I say, we do not care what the duty is so long as prices are not advanced, and as a matter of fact I have known prices to be lower under a tariff than under free trade.
I come now to agriculture, which is the basic industry of this country. May I ask what progress we have made in the last nine years under the administration of the exMinister of Agriculture? How far have we progressed, with all the agricultural students all over the country, and with inspectors grading the farmers of western Canada? Throughout the west you will find a horde of agricultural students running over the country, grading the farmer and his products. Let me mention some of the articles affected. Take hogs: in the different stockyards there are graders grading hogs to the detriment of the farmer. That system was introduced by the late minister. Then you have a system of grading beef in the different packing plants-another system instituted by the hon. gentleman. I wonder whether the hon. gentleman remembers that other system he introduced whereby the packer is allowed to take $2 a head on all male lambs slaughtered. I 22110-167
do not think the little lamb, when he looks at him from the pasture, would feel like following him to school, as the lamb followed Mary. Under the administration of the exMinister of Agriculture, exports of bacon dropped from 120,000,000 pounds to 20,000,000. We are exporting to-day about 20,000,000 pounds of bacon as compared with 120,000,000 pounds in those days.
What did he do in regard to transportation? He inaugurated the Petersen commission, the greatest farce ever placed on record in any parliament. One man, Mr. Symington, drew $10,000 from that commission, and in all it cost the country $35,000 for the effort made to obtain lower freight rates on live stock. All we have received has been the promise to do something. In every newspaper one would pick up there would be found the statement that the rate on li"e stock to the British markets would be reduced from $20 to $15. But nothing has been done to obtain these lower freight rates, except to spend the money of the people.
I remember taking one boat and appealing to the hon. minister to help me out, but what did I get? I got a rate of $27 for space on the Victor, a government owned boat. It is true that that boat sailed to Dundee and not to Liverpool, but I was subjected to a rate of $27 instead of the present rate of $15. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) was not in the house a week until he had obtained a $15 rate on cattle, and to-day a very healthy trade is springing up in the live stock industry because of the present administration. The hon. member spoke about wheat, but he did not say a thing about the live stock industry. I wonder if he looked into the matter while he was in Liverpool? I wonder if he visited any of the markets while he was over there? I did not hear him say that he did; he ignored the industry altogether. He did nothing at all to foster this trade which, along with wheat, is an important basic industry in western Canada.
1 contend that no farmer can be successful unless this live stock industry is fostered. The question is put:	What have you got to
offer, what are you going to do'to aid the agricultural industr}'-? First, I say let us have lower, freight rates. Much attention has been paid to the Crowsnest pass rates, but we had a rate in the old days known as the Manitoba rate which was far lower. The Conservative party was defeated in Manitoba in 1926 because of a most slanderous and diabolical lie which was broadcast to the effect that if Mr. Meighen was elected he

The Budget-Mr. Mullins

would abrogate the Crowsnest pass rate and it would cost the farmers of western Canada $40 for every car of wheat they shipped. That was not the case because Mr. Meighen had no intention whatever of placing a $40 rate on wheat.
I suppose the hon. member knows that Mr. Meighen opposed this rate during the time he was in the house?
He abrogated it.

Mr. Meighen never intended to touch the Crowsnest pass rate in any manner, shape or form. I ask the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown):	Do you
remember anything about the Manitoba rate?
Yes.

Did the hon. member
speak about that rate in his constituency? Did he give the Conservative party any credit for it? Were not those rates much lower? This rate which was taken away in 1918 belonged to us. The Manitoba agreement lowered rates, as compared with the Crowsnest pass rates, by four cents per hundred pounds on grain from all points in Manitoba to Fort William and Port Arthur, and 15 cents on all general merchandise from Fort William and Port Arthur to all points in Manitoba and from all points in Manitoba to Fort William. The Crowsnest pass agreement applied only to limited commodities and in limited territories and on movements in one direction only, whereas the Manitoba contract covered every point in the province and movements east, west, north and south.
On October 6, 1903, an agreement was reached with the Canadian Pacific Railway providing for uniform rates on all railway lines in Manitoba to Fort William, and from Fort William to all points in Manitoba. On October 7, 1903, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company filed with the railway commission its tariff for reduced rates. Those low rates under the Manitoba contract remained in force until March, 1918, when they were overriden by the War Measures Act. In 1919, subsection 5 of the Railway Act was passed in an endeavour to override the Manitoba contract. This subsection was to remain in force for three years, and in June, 1923, an amendment was passed which was to remain in effect until July 6, 1923. The Crowsnest pass contract was never taken into account in connection with rates after the Manitoba contract came into force. Manitoba's contract was taken as a guide for everything. That agreement covered every commodity both coming in and going out of the province.
[Mr. Xluilins.l
The western farmer cannot stand heavy freight rates on commodities coming into and going out of the country, he must have a reduction, and I make an appeal to the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) to give assistance to get commodities out of the country. This is one of the difficulties with which western Canada has to contend. We care very little about the tariff, it is the transportation problem which troubles us. I believe that under the administration of the right hon. gentleman who has charge of the affairs of this country, we will see different and better times in western Canada and for agriculture generally. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take up any more of the time of the house, but I will have something to say later on these matters.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to occupy the attention of the house but for a brief period in order to discuss a very few of the matters dealt with in the budget. The hon. Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) made a speech in the house last Friday in which he dealt with the old age pension issue as it was placed before the people of eastern Canada during the last election campaign. That issue was an exceedingly important one in the campaign because the position taken by the Conservative party undoubtedly resulted in a number of constituencies being carried by that party which otherwise would not have been carried. I think it is most important that there should be no misunderstanding whatever in the minds of any hon. member of this house or of the people of the country as to the exact position taken by the Conservative party in eastern Canada.
First of all, I would like to place on record the plank in the platform of the Conservative party which was adopted in 1927 at the Winnipeg convention. The resolution dealing with old age pensions read as follows:
AVhereas all needy aged persons wherever resident in Canada, qualified by residence have equal right to old age pensions, and
Whereas the present federal pension law is inadequate and unworkable.
Therefore be it resolved that pension legislation should be the subject of federal legislation only.
That, it will be noted, contemplates the establishment of a purely national or federal system of old age pensions, and that was the platform of the Conservative party in eastern Canada during the campaign.
It is yet.

My hon. friend says: "It is
yet;" but the point I wish to make clear and

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
that I will make clear before I finish my remarks on old age pensions, is that there was a second part to that plank and that was that the system was to be inaugurated immediately. The word "immediately" was defined as meaning at the first regular session of parliament. Those were the utterances of responsible leaders of the Conservative party in the maritime provinces, and it was upon those definite promises that they won seats. I think I can make that clear before I resume my seat.
Before I put on record the utterances of the Conservative leaders, I want to refer to one remark that was made by the Minister of Fisheries the other day. He stated I had said in the house, and had misled certain other hon. members by doing so, that he had promised to resign within three months if the old age pension promise was not implemented. If hon. members are interested in the matter and will consult the speech I made, they will find that I said simply that the minister had been reported as stating that it would be put into effect in three months, and I wanted to know whether that was correct or not. He rose in his place and stated that it was not correct. I unreservedly accepted what he said on that point, but I said and I still say that he promised the electors of Nova Scotia that the old age pension legislation by which the federal government would assume the full cost of the burden would be passed at the first regular session of parliament, which is this session. I can prove that by other references.
The Minister of Labour made a speech on this matter of old age pensions in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia. As reported in the Halifax Herald of June 24 of last year, he said:
Again Senator Robertson referred to the Conservative convention at Winnipeg, and to the unanimous endorsation given by that convention to the proposal to establish a purely federal system of old age pensions, the cost of which would be entirely borne by the federal treasury.
"The present act is nothing but a piecemeal proposition," he said. "Are you going to be content to pay your share of the pensions of the old people of British Columbia, while your own aged people are getting nothing?"
"The King government," said Senator Robertson, "paid out in old age pensions last year about $2,000,000. Previous to that they discontinued the Agricultural Aid Act, the Technical Education Act and the federal aid to highways, all of which were established by the previous administration, thus saving about $6,000,000 a year. And yet Mr. King, after taking $6,000,000 from the people of Canada, is now offering them a sop of $2,000,000 in old age pensions, and is saying to the Canadian working man "after you are 70 years of age we will pay half of a pension of $20 a month for you."
Two or three months ago the present Minister of Labour made a speech in another place, and that speech was mentioned in the press of the maritime provinces. A telegram was sent to him by a Conservative paper there and this is the telegram which he sent in reply as published in that paper:
No change in Prime Minister's intention regarding old age pensions legislation. Impression gone abroad that legislation providing for dominion administration to be passed at this session. In my opinion this quite impossible-
Why does he say "impossible"?	.
-because of the jurisdictional question-
Yet the jurisdictional issue was ridiculed by hon. gentlemen opposite in the last campaign. -having to be first adjusted by agreement with provinces and confirmed by provincial enactment. This does not, however, prevent the provinces continuing to administer and the federal government paying the larger [DOT] proportion of total cost. Expect amendments to existing act probably made this session, but not to extent of providing for dominion administration until necessary preliminary matters have been discussed and settled with provinces. Prime Minister's public forecast holds good.
But what I suggest is that' between the assumption of office by this government and the present time there has been abundant opportunity for those preliminary matters to have been discussed and settled. So much for the Minister of Labour.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) spoke on this matter repeatedly in the maritime provinces. The first speech he made was on July 2, at Yarmouth, as reported in the Halifax Herald of July 3, at page 5, column 6. This is what he said:
"If the Conservative government succeeds on July 28, and I have every reason to believe it will," Mr. Bennett exclaimed, "I will see to it that old age pensions are paid to every province of the dominion from the federal treasury."
When the Prime Minister made the statement-
If the Conservative government succeeds on July 28, I will see to it that old age pensions are paid-
-he meant if and when the Conservative party gets into power he did not mean at some future time and any person hearing that utterance would place no other interpretation upon it.
The present Prime Minister proceeded to Halifax where he made a speech on July 3, which was reported in the Halifax Herald of July 4. A summary of what the Prime Minister said in that speech in reference to this and other matters was published on the first page of that paper. He said:
As an earnest of his sincerity, Mr. Bennett made it plain that every maritime Conservative
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

member who is elected on July 28th would be at perfect liberty to vote in parliament against him and his government if he failed to carry out to the letter the definite pledges he gave last night, among which were the following of vital importance to the people of Nova Scotia:
1.	Dominion cooperation in the construction of the Halifax harbour bridge as a national obligation in relation to a national port.
2.	The immediate payment of old age pensions to the people of Nova Scotia and the other provinces of Canada 100 per cent from the dominion treasury as a duty the dominion owes its needy people who are unable to provide for themselves.
The Prime Minister proceeded to other points in the province where he made similar speeches. At Antigonish on July 9, as reported in the Halifax Herald of July 10, he said:
Jn detail Hon. Mr. Bennett outlined to his audience the pledge of the Conservative party to provide a system of old age pensions, the cost of which will be borne entirely by the federal treasury.
There are other quotations from the Prime Minister which I could put on record, but I think these will suffice. I come now to the speeches made-and there were many of them-by the distinguished gentleman who now holds the portfolio of Fisheries in this government and who at that time was Premier of Nova Scotia. He began his campaign at Stewiacke in t'he county of Colchester just outside my constituency. His speech, which was delivered on June 25, was very fully reported in the Halifax Herald, the party organ for the province of Nova Scotia on July 26, and from it I quote the following:
I say the federal government can pay old age pensions. If they can pay 50 per cent is it illegal for them to pay 99 per cent?
A little later on he said:
The Conservative party has solemnly pledged itself to pay the entire cost of old age pensions. ... I believe they will carry out this pledge, and if they do not, I will join with you in voting against them on this measure.
At Aberdeen Beach in my constituency on the 10th day of June, the then premier of Nova Scotia, the present Minister of Fisheries, made a speech which was reported as follows in the Halifax Herald of July 10, 1930, page 2:
Speaking of the position of the Conservatives on old age pensions. Premier Rhodes said that they should be a national obligation.
Then comes perhaps the most emphatic speech of all, made in the town in which I ' have the privilege of residing, before a very large audience, a meeting of three or four thousand people. Those who heard the speech were greatly impressed by it; many of
[Mr. Ilsley.1
them discussed it in relation to old age pensions in my hearing, so that I have a pretty accurate and direct personal knowledge of what the present Minister of Fisheries said in respect to old age pensions in the province of Nova Scotia. This speech was made on July 16 in Kentville, Kings county, and was reported in the Halifax Herald of July 17, 1980, on page 5, the last column:
In referring to old age pensions Mr. Rhodes said: "Mr. King in Liberal Prince Edward Island was prepared to consider federal payment in full, but in Nova Scotia he met the constitutional bugbear and could not pay more than 50 per cent."
The Conservative party stood pledged to institute a system of federal old age pensions at the first regular session of parliament, Mr. Rhodes said, and he continued: "If the Conservative party does not implement that pledge I will retire from public life forever."
Now I submit that there may be circumstances, exceptional circumstances, that sometimes justify public men in not keeping their bounden express pledges-circumstances of a most extreme character. But let us have no misunderstanding in this house about what was promised. If the Conservative government of the day is taking the position that it has to break a promise because of exceptional conditions, let it frankly come out and say so, but do not let us have any misunderstanding about what was promised the people of the maritime provinces in this matter of old age pensions. They were promised in the most express and the most solemn terms that they would get old age pensions in full from this government at the first regular session, and the present Minister of Fisheries said that if that were not done he would retire from public life forever.
Another matter that is perhaps of some interest to the people of Nova Scotia particularly is that of the so-called national fuel policy, concerning which there are certain provisions in the budget. This policy may be divided into two parts, first the rail subventions, and second, increased duties. My own opinion about this policy is that the rail subventions may result in the movement of certain additional quantities of coal. It would be strange if they did not. In some respects the subventions are reduced, but in other respects they are increased, and the public of Canada will be paying larger sums than heretofore to encourage the movement of coal. We naturally expect, therefore, that there will be some additional movement of coal, not a very great additional movement. A few hundred thousand tons will be the limit, as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) pointed out; and there is no member of this house better qualified to judge

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
accurately of the effect of subventions than the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth, because, as a member of the Mackenzie King administration, he took a particular interest in the working out of the order in council in 1927 and 1928 under which hundreds of thousands of tons of coal have already been moved. Regarding these subventions, Mr. Speaker, I have very little to say in the way of criticism, but I do say that when public men on the Conservative side of politics in the maritime provinces speak about the subventions in this budget as the launching of a national fuel policy they are talking the veriest nonsense. These subventions are merely an adaptation of the subventions provided for in 1927 and 1928. They are simply minor additions to the fuel policy which was put into effect by the King government in 1927 and 1928.
When we come to the second part of the national fuel policy, the provisions for additional duties, different principles apply, but I warn such hon. members as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Smith), who made a very fair speech the other day on this subject, and prominent -men on the Conservative side of politics in the province of Nova Scotia who are speaking on this question, not to expect too much from the very small increases in. duties that are provided for in this budget. I suppose that if there is one hon. member in this house on the Conservative side who knows more than others about matters pertaining to coal and steel it is the hon. member whom I am glad to see in his seat now, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley). He has spent his life in the coal and steel industries. Compared with his knowledge of the subject, the knowledge of the hon. Minister of Fisheries is rudimentary, and it would be so admitted by himself, I am sure. The hon. member for Pictou is in a position to state pretty accurately what would be the effect of particular duties, and I want to refer the house to a speech made by him on May 17, 1926, which will be found at page 3422 of the Hansard of that year. He said, and I invite attention particularly to the concluding part of his remarks:
We should first impose upon coal a duty sufficient to enable us to control our own market. We should have an adequate protective duty on all classes of coal, coke and patent fuel's equal to, say, not less than 25 per cent of the present laid down, c.i.f. cost. That would be, say, $1.25 to $1.50 a ton, the duty to apply to all coal, coke and patent fuel imported irrespective of its origin or the purpose for which it may be used. I have said that the rate should be $1.50 a ton and if it w ere that duty would be considerably lower than that at one time imposed by the people of the United States on Nova Scotia coal then largely shipped and sold by us to New England
cities. Some of my hon. friends may balk at a duty of $1.50 a ton. While the industry is certainly entitled to that amount of protection I wish to emphasize the fact that a rate of duty less than one dollar a ton applied to all classes of fuel will entirely fail of its object, be mischievous and disappointing.
This is the utterance of the best authority on the government side of the house on this matter of coal, and if those are the views of the hon. member for Pictou to-day, I think he owes it to his constituency, to his province and to the country, to tell them that this 75 cents a ton duty will entirely fail of its object, be mischievous and disappointing.
Let me come to two other features of the budget which I wish to discuss, namely the measures designed to afford some additional protection to the grain growers of the west.
I think protection is the right term, because these measures are essentially protective in their nature. The first is the five cents a bushel bonus on the export of wheat. Let me say quite emphatically that I am opposed to that provision; I am opposed to the provision of five cents a bushel as a bonus on export wheat. My reasons for that opposition are as follows: In the first place, it is a discriminatory selection of one commodity. In Canada wheat is not the only exporting industry. As I have repeatedly said, we have most important exporting industries in the province of Nova Scotia. We have industries which at various times become in a very depressed condition. There were four or five moist unfavourable years for apple growers in Nova Scotia a few years ago. Last year was better, but for a few years before that, due to unfavourable crop and market conditions, the apple growers of Nova Scotia were going behind. What justice is there in picking out one agricultural commodity, wheat, and paying a bonus of five cents a bushel on export, and not doing the same thing with regard to other agricultural products? The right hon. the Prime Minister may say:	Yes, but the
wheat growing industry is the biggest industry of Canada. My answer is that it is not as big an industry as agriculture itself. If it is fair to bonus one class of export it is fair to bonus them all. When a year or two ago the United States were trying tr. evolve a plan which would offset the deleterious effect of the protective tariff upon the agricultural industry, they did not apply their export debenture plan to wheat alone, they applied it to other commodities as well. So my first point of objection to the five cent bonus is that it is unjust discrimination against other branches of agriculture.
My second point is that it still further accentuates the discrimination in freight rate*
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

against domestic purchasers. That subject has been dealt with in this house by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) and by other hon. members. The situation that exists in western Canada was graphically described by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) the other day, when he said that poultry raisers and others there were contemplating the importation of wheat from Australia rather than pay the very oppressive domestic freight rates which are so much higher than the export rates. That situation exists also in eastern Canada. This provision in the budget still further accentuates the discrimination between export and domestic freight rates.
My third objection is that this five cent bonus on wheat invites reprisals of a most disastrous kind. A year or two ago when the United States congress was discussing the export debenture plan it looked as if that plan would be crystallized into legislation, and that the exporters of farm products were about to receive a bonus amounting to half the customs tariff rates upon the commodities that they exported. When that stage was reached I received most earnest protests from exporters in my constituency because they knew they would be prejudiced, if not ruined, in attempting to place their apples on the British market in competition with American apples. Now, this legislation is on the same principle as the export debenture plan, although it does not go quite so far. No wonder American newspapers are already talking about the revival of the export debenture plan. Time, a magazine published in New York, contains the following in to-day's issue:
Subsidy No. 1 is a Canadian treasury bounty of 5 cents on each bushel of Canadian export wheat. Thus in selling his wheat abroad the Canadian farmer will have a five c-ut edge over his United States competitor. This provision is likely to stir another demand in congress for the export debenture whereunder United States wheat growers would get a bounty of 50 per cent of the tariff rate (i.e. 21 cents) for every bushel of wheat they sold outside the country.
Therefore, I say, Mr. Speaker, that we should not encourage dumping when we condemn the practice by other countries, and talk about it in a tone of great moral earnestness as something which should be severely reprobated.
The other protective feature of the budget, designed I suppose to assist western agriculture-I do not know what other reason there could be for it

is the proposed duty on Indian corn. I got from the Department of Trade and Commerce not very long ago trade returns to find out where we get our corn. 
A great deal of it comes from the Argentine republic. I find that during the last ten years our trade with the Argentine has been more or less onesided, that we are selling to them a great deal more than we are buying from them every year. During the last five years we have sold them about $68,000,000 worth of goods, and we have purchased from them only about $40,000,000. Of the commodities that we buy from the Argentine republic the most important is corn; it accounts for considerably more than half our total imports from that country. This government has destroyed our trade with Russia by the absurd embargo on Russian goods; they have destroyed our trade with New Zealand by their stubborn adherence to an eight cent duty against the advice of those in the dairy industry who should know what they are talking about; now apparently they are on the highroad to destroy our trade with the Argentine republic. I submit that we should be devising ways and means of encouraging importations from the Argentine rather than discouraging them. What is the use of sending a good will mission to the Argentine, if immediately after their return we impose this duty against one of their principal exports to Canada? What is the use of putting expensive machinery into the port of Halifax for the handling of Argentine corn? The hon. members for Halifax know all about that. What is the use of doing it if we are going to destroy that trade? And the destruction of that trade is not going to help us in this country. I have received letters from those in my constituency who raise pork, beef and poultry, protesting against this duty. They have to have this Argentine corn. They are a long way from western barley. The freight rates on western barley are very, very high, and they assure me most positively that Indian corn from the Argentine republic is absolutely necessary if they are going to get the best results in the feeding of their stock. The 20 cents a bushel duty, according to the best figures that I can get, will place a burden upon Nova Scotian feeders alone of between $150,000 and $175,000 a year. I protest against this proposal. I say it is absurd and suicidal, and I cannot understand why the government inserted it in the budget.
There is another matter that I desire to refer to, and I do so with some diffidence, but with a feeling that it deserves the attention of every hon. member-the duty on that very necessary commodity, gasoline. Gasoline is used everywhere. It is almost as necessary as bread, I was going to say. It enters into the life of the people at every turn. We all

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
use it-gasoline. Now, let me point out something that may surprise hon. members. The duty on gasoline, when you add the tariff rates to the dumping duty, is over 1Q0 per cent ad valorem. I wonder if hon. members realize that? I will give the house the figures on which that is based. The Department of National Revenue divides the United States, where we get practically all our crude oil and some of our refined gasoline, into nine districts. One is Pennsylvania, New York and district, which includes the Atlantic seaboard. They fix the valuation for duty purposes in that district at 6-672 cents per wine gallon. In Toledo, Detroit, Cleveland and district the value for duty purposes is 7-285. And so it goes on down the list. I am sorry I have not time to give fuller details. But the point is that a different value for duty purposes is placed upon the refined gasoline that comes from each of these nine districts in the United States. I will explain how that works out. Suppose an importer in the city of Toronto is bringing in United States motor gasoline, 58-60, from a western Pennsylvania refinery. Appraiser's bulletin 3715, issued June 5, 1931, to which I refer, fixes the valuation at 6-672 cents per wine gallon; add one-fifth to convert into the imperial gallon, and you have the valuation for duty purposes per imperial gallon at 8-006 cents. The National Petroleum News, in its issue of June 3, 1931, gives the value at the refineries in western Pennsylvania at 4-875 cents per wine gallon. If you add one-fifth to that you find that the value per Canadian gallon at the Pennsylvania refineries is 5-85 cents. The department's value being 8-006 cents, and the real value being 5-85 cents, the difference is the dumping duty, which amounts to 2-156 cents. If you add that to the 2-5 cents of tariff duty, you have 4-656 cents as the actual, real duty on gasoline brought from Pennsylvania to Toronto. In other words, on a product worth 5-85 cents a gallon, you have a duty of 4-656 cents, or 78 per cent. I could place similar figures on record to show that gasoline brought from the mid-continent field, which is the fundamental field, carries an ad valorem duty of 122 per cent, so that averaging the two fields, the rate is over 100 per cent ad valorem.
It has been said that the refineries are not taking advantage of that duty. They are taking advantage of it, and if I had time I could show by figures which I do not think can be controverted to the extent of a fraction of a cent, that the wholesale price to Canadian refineries, for gasoline delivered in tank cars at Toronto, is 3-522 cents higher than the price for which those same importers
could get their gasoline in the United States, freight, sales tax and special import tax paid. In other words, they are using the dumping duty, plus the tariff duty, to keep their price up by something over 3i cents. I am told, though I have not been able to check the information, that the difference is greater in other parts of Canada, and that one would be perfectly safe in saying that the wholesale price is 4 cents a gallon greater than it would be but for the duty. On the 600,000,000 gallons of gasoline used in a year by the Canadian consumers this tax, levied for the benefit of the refineries, amounts to $24,000,000. .
When it gets to the retail price the difference is very much greater. Let us take the retail figures, with all the taxes, the state tax on one side and the provincial tax on the other, stripped off. A comparison of prices from coast to coast in Canada and the United States gives the following figures, per imperial gallon in both cases, as the retail prices of gasoline, omitting provincial road taxes, in effect June 1, 1931, as published in the National Petroleum News of June 3, 1931, pages 92 and 93:
