There is an average difference of over 7 cents a gallon in the retail price across the United States on one side of the boundary line, and the price across Canada on the other side, and that difference is due to the tariff and the dumping duty. I submit no other explanation is reasonable, and no other explanation can be made to fit the case. I do not know what hon. members of this, house think about this situation. Here is an industry which employes 5,000 people and pays out $8,000,000 yearly in wages and salaries, according to the last bulletin issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce. That industry gets from $20,000,000 to $25,000,000 in excess prices from the people of Canada. Every fisherman who has a little gasoline boat in a cove on the bay of Fundy; every farmer who has a truck; every man or woman of moderate means who has a small car, pays,

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
by virtue of the tariff, between three and four cents a gallon for the benefit of these refining companies, some of which are more than half owned by foreign interests, since the oil refining business in Canada is largely controlled by the Standard Oil.
I submit that this is a case for the exercise of the powers which were taken by the Prime Minister and his government last September. If we read the debates of that day we will find that it was not laid down simply that if the price went up these powers would be exercised; it was promised by the Prime Minister that these powers would be exercised if there came about too great a discrepancy between the price here and the price abroad, showing that the duty was being used by the home producers in order to keep up prices beyond what they would be otherwise by reason of the interference with the free play of economic forces. These promises were made last September, and I submit that these powers should be exercised now. If these figures are wrong, let the oil companies come forward with an explanation. Do not let them do what one gentleman did in this morning's paper, simply accuse an hon. member of the house of not knowing what he was talking about. Let them give an explanation. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) made an extremely able statement the other night, going into the financial structure of these companies. He showed that the greatest abuses exist which permit these companies to exploit and plunder the people of this country through the tariff. The government should take action in this matter, or at least the oil companies should state why the government should not take action, because a prima facie case has been made out against them which calls for the exercise of the powers taken by the government in their legislation of last September.

speakeroldname: Mr. L. W. JOHNSTONE (Cape Breton North-Victoria):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up much of the time of the house in connection with this debate, since the budget has been thoroughly discussed from every angle by many hon. members, particularly with regard to the subject of coal, in which I am particularly interested. That matter has been ably discussed by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes) and also by my hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Smith), so that repetition on my part at this time is uncalled for.
However, before the discussion ends I wish to offer my congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) for the very splendid budget he brought down this year. For some 
years I have been studying our Canadian budgets; I have heard five budgets read in this house and have studied a great many more, but I have never understood a budget so thoroughly as I understood the one brought down this year. It explained the condition of affairs in Canada as it never has been explained before, and I am sure it must be gratifying to the Minister of Finance to have his budget so well received by the people of Canada. We have captains of industry, manufacturers, presidents of coal mines, and the president of our coal union of the United Mine Workers of Cape Breton, giving the budget a very favourable reception and looking for something to come out of this policy for which the country has been waiting so long.
I am a protectionist, and I took my first lesson in 1878, at a political meeting at which Sir Charles Tupper announced his national policy. I was only a young fellow at the time, but I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I was very much impressed by the views expressed by Sir Charles Tupper on that occasion. He was making a tour of Canada, commencing in the city of Sydney in the east and going right across the dominion. At that time, as hon. members know, the country was in a state of very serious depression, and conditions were worse than they are to-day. The question which was being discussed then seems to be equally important to-day. At that time it was not merely a matter of free trade versus protection; it was a question of industrial life or death, and I believe the situation is the same to-day. The coal mines were not working at that time. There was only one working in the southern and one in the northern part of the island. Sir Charles Tupper declared that the day would come when steel works and coal mines would be numerous throughout Cape Breton island, and a duty on coal was imposed. A brief history of the Nova Scotia coal industry might be interesting. In the year 1879 the province of Nova Scotia produced a total of 866,220 tons. These figures, by the way, are from the records of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. In the following year, 1880, the duty was raised from 50 to 60 cents a ton and in that year the production of the Nova Scotia mines jumped to 1,777,669 tons, or more than double the output of the previous year. That was the greatest comparative increase in the history of Nova Scotia's production in any one year since confederation. It shows what can be done by an increase in the duty on coal.
Members from Cape Breton have in the last five years been endeavouring to solve the coal problem. We have brought forward

The Budget-Mr. Johnstone
several proposed solutions but they do not seem to have materialized. We tried to get. the people of Canada to use coke instead of hard coal, and I am sure that if anyone would use coke manufactured from Nova Scotia coal instead of using hard coal, that person would never use coal again. Coke is cleaner, freer, gives a better fire, and altogether involves less trouble in its use. The coke bill, of course, was of no advantage to us, because coal was coming in free; and the rebate on slack coal brought in for coke purposes made impossible a solution so far as we in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, were concerned.
The miners of Cape Breton have been looking for some time for something of this nature. Clouds have been hanging over the heads of the miners. Starvation has been staring them in the face in many instances, and work seemed to be getting scarcer every day. But a ray of sunshine came to them, a gleam of hope, when the Prime Minister, on his political tour, announced publicly that he would institute a fuel policy. He has taken the first step in the direction of such a policy, and I may say here, Mr. Speaker, that it is not surprising that within the last week men who are opposed politically to the right hon. gentleman and his government should get up on the platform in my own county and say emphatically that the budget was worthless to the coal industry. These men might at least have allowed our people to derive some encouragement from the budget. There was no necessity for them to attempt to discourage our miners. Whatever the result may be. we do not know, but we hope for the best. And after all, what have these men who talk that way to say with respect to the record of their government? What their government did at that time was simply to lower the duties on coal and to insert in the tariff certain schedules providing for a series of drawbacks the effect of which was that the duty was reduced almost to the vanishing point. What has the present government done in its short period of office so far as coal is concerned? It has imposed a duty of 75 cents specific, the highest duty in the history of Canada. It has removed anthracite from the free list and imposed a duty of 40 cents a ton; it has taken coke off the free list and imposed a duty of SI; it has imposed a duty of $7.50 on charcoal; and it has prevented Russian coal from coming in, and thrown up safeguards against the dumping of coal into Canada. Notwithstanding this, these men declare that the budget is worthless to the coal industry.
It seems to me that we have too much politics in Canada. I do not see why a government which has just come into power should be subject to abuse when it brings down a budget containing certain provisions that will improve the condition of things in the country. Why should the opposition indulge in such criticism before they see what the actual results are? Here is something which we have been endeavouring for nine years to get in the coal industry. We have it to-day. I say to my hon. friends, why not wait and see the result of this? A year from now, two years from now, will be plently of time to criticize this budget, when we find out exactly where we stand. There is no use in abusing it to-day. I do not expect to see any immediate effect: our contracts are all made already. But I do believe that the subventions this year will assist us materially in our coal trade in Cape Breton.
Years before confederation coke was coming into Canada free, while we were selling Nova Scotia coal in the United States under a duty of $1.75 a ton. That was the condition of affairs when the great statesman Haliburton came to Nova Scotia on his tour of the dominion. He made a prophecy then, for apparently he had a vision. He asked,-"How is it that coal is coming free into Canada while you are sending coal into the United States under a duty of $1.75, when you have a beautiful waterway, the St. Lawrence, whereby every ton of coal could be shipped to other parts of Canada? Canals will be built on which you can carry your coal to the west". At that time there was not a ton of coal being shipped on the St. Lawrence, nor was there a canal in Canada. To-day the St. Lawrence has been made a perfect waterway for the largest steamships in the world, many of them filled with coal. This has all come about through the national policy announced in 1878 by Sir John Macdonald.
I am a firm believer in protection and in interprovincial reciprocal trade. I might quote the words of Mr. Burnaby, trade commissioner for the maritime provinces, addressing the border cities chamber of commerce the other day. He said:
We cannot be expected to bear up our end in building a nation unless we can sell our products.
Then he set forth the principle of interprovincial trade, urging the largest possible development of such trade to the mutual benefit of every province and to the Dominion as a whole. The only way in which Canada can be built up is to protect her industries, her raw materials and natural resources, and to allow in free of duty those commodities which we cannot produce. Our raw materials are being sent out of the country to be

The Budget-Mr. Johnstone
manufactured and then are being returned as finished articles. There is a very good example right in my own constituency. The Liberal government of some years ago entered into a contract with an American firm to lease twelve hundred thousand acres of pulpwood land at a very small rental, I think no more than $6,000 per year. This lease was for ninety-nine years, and year after year, month after month, large steamers are going out of Ste. Ann's bay filled with pulpwood for the United States. Our forests are being devastated because no effort is being made to plant new trees. But that is not the worst of it. There is being sent out of the country our greatest asset, our young men and women. These young people have been educated at the expense of the Canadian ratepayers, and they are following this pulpwood in order to take part in its manufacture in the United States. Why not keep that pulpwood in Canada to be manufactured here by our own people? Ever since 1878 I have been in favour of adopting this course, and I shall continue to be in favour during the few remaining years of my life.
I have great faith in the policies of the present administration. I have great faith in the budget which the Minister of Finance has brought down. The people of Canada should unite to make this country a great nation. Under the policies brought down by the Minister of Finance Canada can become an independent nation and derive the benefits of her own wealth; she can become independent rather than being dependent upon the United States.

Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to continue unduly the discussion on the budget as I believe this matter should be disposed of so that the house can take up other matters still to come before it to the end that the session may soon be brought to a. conclusion. However, representing as I do one of the coal counties in the province of Nova Scotia-the county which has been mining and exporting coal possibly longer than any other county in Canada-I feel that it is incumbent upon me to give thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) for the interest he has shown in the coal industry by increasing the duties on coal. My thanks are due to him, as are the thanks Of the miners of the province, not only for the increased duties but also for the rail subvention on coal. I have no doubt that these changes will go a great way towards increasing our markets in the central provinces.
" Speaking in the house this afternoon the hbn. member for Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley)

was good enough to make some very complimentary remarks in regard to myself and my knowledge of the steel and coal business. He devoted some time to quoting a speech which he says I made in 1926. It is quite likely that I did speak along the lines he intimated. I was a young man at that time; let me hope I have learned something since. The duties on coal are not as high as I should like to have them, but I am very glad, as are the people of my province, to know that the budget provides considerable increases in the coal duties. These are the highest duties on coal we have ever had, but I hope they do not mark the limit in that regard.
In 1925, under the regime of our hon. friends opposite, the effective duty on bituminous coal was reduced to 50 cents per ton for both run of mine and slack, anthracite and coke being put on the free list. That was the situation in regard to coal duties on June 1, when the Prime Minister by his budget proposals raised the duty to 75 cents per ton, on soft coal, including run of mine, slack and screenings; on anthracite to 40 cents per ton and on coke to one dollar per ton. Not only have the duties been raised, but an embargo lias been placed on Russian coal and an increase has been granted in the rail subvention. In addition to these measures, provision has been made to guard against the dumping of American coal at slaughter prices. I submit that these actions make a good beginning, and the miners of Nova Scotia accept them as such. I never had any doubt as to the honesty of the Prime Minister's intentions in the further protection of the coal producers in eastern, central and western Canada; neither had I any doubt that no undue delay would occur in the bringing down of effective tariff legislation to that end, and my faith has been justified.
Personally, I should have liked to see the Prime Minister go much further in dealing with the iron and steel industry, but I realize his difficulty and the tremendous pressure of work which confronted him. I can assure him that the people of the maritimes appreciate the situation and applaud the action which he has already taken, believing as they do that such action will result in great advantage to the coal mining industry which contributes so largely to our prosperity. No other prime minister of Canada has had to face a similar situation, and in view of these conditions we are prepared to wait for another year at which time we hope further assistance will be given to the iron and steel industries.
I regret that the former Minister of National Revenue, the hon. member for North Waterloo

The Budget-Mr. Cantley
(Mr. Euler) is not in his seat. I have a great deal of respect for the hon. member. His views on most questions are reasonable. His views on fiscal matters march closely with those held by hon. members on this side of the house, and because of his ordinarily good judgment on other questions, I was much surprised the other day,to hear him express his views in connection with the action taken by the government with regard to Russian trade. I have no sympathy with the suggestion that Canada should sever trade relations with the Soviet government because of its repudiation of God and its contempt for religion. The Lord God of Hosts still reigns, His arm is not shortened and, in His own good time and way He will deal with Russia. My approval of the action of the government in placing an embargo on trade with Soviet Russia is based upon quite different reasons. Russia occupies in Europe an area corresponding with the position of Canada on the American continent. Russia's products are the same as ours-wheat, other agricultural products, lumber, coal. In these we are competitors and always will be. What, therefore, have we to gain by trade with them? Can we or should our people be asked to compete with the labour of serfs whose standard of living and social relations are barely, if at all, above those of the beasts of the field. It is on these grounds that I applaud the action of the government, and for the same reason the people of Canada will judge the government as to its decision and action in that matter.
For the first time since becoming a member of this house, I had on June 1 the privilege of hearing a real budget speech, with a full statement of our national fiscal position, a complete balance sheet of the dominion given parliament by the right hon., the Finance Minister, before stating his proposals for meeting the situation confronting us and providing the necessary revenue to meet the country's immediate, pressing needs.
As to the remarks of the financial critic of the opposition, successful advocate and experienced debater as he is, when I listened to his criticism of the budget proposals of the finance minister, when I recalled the eloquent and powerful speech made by him in this chamber a few years ago, on which occasion he spoke with conviction based on uncontrovertible facts, and when I recalled his then confident assurance and joy of battle as contrasted with his lack of enthusiasm for the task assigned him by his leader, I confess he had .my sympathy. Frankly I thought the speech unworthy of him, containing as it did no valid or worth while opposition to the
budget proposals suggested-a two and a quarter hour sermon on the text "Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?"-and finally coming down to the wail of a dissatisfied child who wishes to express his misery, although conscious that little attention will be paid to his bewailing.
My honourable, bluenose friend, the exMinister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) played with a matter of percentages when dealing with the sales tax; he stated that the budget now before the house had raised the sales tax 400 per cent. True, but it is also true that the government of which he was a member raised the sales tax 100 per cent. That 100 per cent increase was a much greater increase than the 400 per cent of which he now complains, because they then doubled the sales tax, raised it from 3 per cent to 6 per cent, whereas the proposal before the house increases the rate from 1 per cent to 4 per cent, so that the sales tax to-day is but two-thirds of that imposed by the government of which my hon. friend was a member. He suggests the 4 per cent tax will bring in 52 millions of dollars. If that be true, then the 6 per cent tax of my friends opposite brought in $48,990,076. more than the 52 millions- he estimates for the present year's tax. This is evident from the fact that for the year ended March 31. 1924, the sum of $100,990,076 was collected by way of sales tax under the government of my hon. friends opposite.
My hon. friend put on Hansard, as reported at page 2296, a quotation from a reported speech of an English economist, with the dictum that high tariffs stimulate the growth of nationalism. Is that a fault? Is that anything that we in Canada need fear? With a dominion continent-wide, with diversity of races, language, occupations, trades and markets, is the growth of nationalism to be condemned?
The hon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth welcomed any tangible assistance to the coal industry, but he did not think the increased duty would give the industry of Nova Scotia practically any additional advantage. Let us review the tariff history of the coal trade since confederation.
From the inception of confederation, 1876 to 1879, those years, coal was on the free list. In 1879 the Conservative finance minister imposed a duty of 50 cents per ton on anthracite and 60 cents on bituminous coal, with 20 per cent on coal dust. In 1886 anthracite was placed on the free list, the 60 cents on bituminous remaining, with 20 per cent on coal dust. In November of the following year, 1887, anthracite coal dust was placed
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

on the free list by order in council, the mistaken reason given being that anthracite coal dust was not a competitor of Canadian-mined coal, though it certainly was then as now being largely used for steam boiler fuel.
No further change was made until 1890. Anthracite coal dust then remained free as in 1887 with 60 cents per ton on bituminous, 20 per cent on soft coal dust, with anthracite, including screenings, on the free list. These duties remained until 1897, when under the first Fielding budget the duty on bituminous coal was reduced from 60 cents to 53 cents, while the duty on such bituminous slack coal as would pass through a one-half inch screen was placed at 13 cents per ton. For ten years no further change was made until the Fielding budget in 1907, which retained all classes of anthracite on the free list, continued the duty of 53 cents on bituminous under the general tariff, but reduced it to 45 cents under the intermediate and 35 cents under the British preferential tarif, and fixed the rate on bituminous slack at 14 cents with the intermediate at 12 cents and the British preference at 10 cents per ton.
These rates continued unaltered until 1924, when (he King government reduced the general tariff on bituminous to 50 cents, raising slack fo the same level, which remained in force until now changed by the proposals of the leader of the government. By the proposals of the finance minister, the duty on bituminous coal and coal dust of all kinds has been raised to 75 cents general, with a tax of 40 cents per ton on anthracite and SI per ton on coke. Hard coal from Great Britain remains on the free list. These latter coal duties are the highest so far imposed in Canada on foreign fuel.
This, Mr. Speaker, I submit is a fairly good start in the direction of a national fuel policy. That is the gift horse which the official critic of the opposition does not care to look in the mouth. I suggest he would prefer that the gift horse did not appear at all; indeed, his amendment now before the house, if adopted, would dispose of the horse and the major advantage we are getting from the tariff. That is the situation so far as he is concerned, and that is his view as expressed by the amendment which he has moved.
But the financial critic's political friends do not ali agree with him, for here is a Cape Breton paper's report on whait the mayor of North Sydney thinks of the coal duties:
Mayor Kelly of North Sydney is credited with having stated at least week's meeting of the town council that the Bennett budget was the best budget for Cape Breton ever submitted to parliament. The value of this testi-

mony is that it comes from one who knows, and who has no strong bias in favour of the Conservative party. It is a view which is shared by practically everyone in Cape Breton.
That is Mayor Kelly's view of the budget, and may I remind the hon. gentleman that Mr. Kelly was for some years the representative of his county in the parliament of Canada, sitting with my friends opposite. The value of this testimony is that it comes from one who knows, one who can safely be said to have no strong bias in favour of the Conservative party.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I had referred to the statement of Mayor Kelly of North Sydney, that the Bennet budget was the best budget for Cape Breton ever submitted to parliament. I propose now to turn to the reaction to the budget of the American anthracite coal operators who have hitherto found so large a market for their product in Canada.
That the new duties will be effective in reducing the sale of American coal in Canada is evidenced by the attacks now being made by American coal producers on Nova Scotia coal and coke in a statement recently issued and now being circulated, which says in part: The tests show that American anthracite is a much more efficient and economical fuel than either Welsh coal or coke, and that at current prices the use of Pennsylvania anthracite means a saving of $1.75 a ton to the householder when actual heating value is considered.
The statement is, to use the words of an eminent British statesman "a frigid and calculated lie." Those who have had experience with all types of fuel available in Canada may be permitted not only to doubt this assertion, but to challenge it definitely and positively. Tests carried out under official auspices and supervision have shown that Nova Scotia coke is superior to American anthracite, that it does better work at less cost. The results of these tests, well known to our people, merely confirm the experience of those who have used both Nova Scotia coke and American anthracite. We welcome every comparison of these types of fuel, confident that where Nova Scotia coke is given an opportunity to demonstrate its real value, it will be proven not only equal to but better than the best of any other variety of domestic fuel. The results in the Nova Scotia schools, where imported anthracite has been replaced by Nova Scotia coke, are perfectly satisfying both in economics and heating value. Through displacement of anthracite coal by Nova Scotia coke thousands of dollars are being saved every year.
Now, if the coal mining industry of Canada is to be saved from disaster, a protective duty is needed on all forms of fuel, whether they be bituminous or anthracite coal or coke. To be effective, the duty should not be less than $1 a ton. I am content for the moment with the increase to 75 cents on bituminous coal and to a dollar on coke. But I hope to see the day not far distant when the protection will be increased to at least a dollar a ton. Viewed from the standpoint of protection offered most Canadian industries over
a long period of time, the coal trade is entitled to protection of at least $1.50 a ton. Further, the rebate of duty on bituminous coal, as provided for by items 1019, 1049, 1065 and 1066, should be cancelled, and with their cancellation should disappear the subvention paid the Nova Scotia coal, industry, which for part of the fiscal year 1930-31 amounted to $135,209.23. May I point out that the coal and coke imported during the fiscal year 1930-31 totalled 18.311,521 tons, of which Great Britain supplied 1,081,070 tons. A duty of one dollar per ton on all the coal and coke imported, with a preference of 25 per cent in favour of Great Britain, would have provided a revenue of $18,041,235.50, as compared with the duty collected in 1930-31 of $6,916,098, less drawbacks of $1,157,679.43, or a net revenue from the coal duties of $5,758,418.57. The increase in revenue would be $12,282,816.93, to which could be added the saving due to cancellation of the subvention paid on Nova Scotia coal used in iron and steel production, which for the portion of 1930-31 was $135,209.23 as I already stated. This would give an increase in revenue of, say, $12,418,026.16. The additional revenue is needed. Why not secure it when it can be obtained without imposing any unfair or undue burden on either domestic consumers or manufacturers? Of course, I realize that the revenue from this source would diminish in proportion as the duty was effective in replacing foreign by domestic fuel.
May I point out that the Nova Scotia iron and steel industry now pays duties ranging from 10, 15 to 25 per cent on such items as caustic magnesite, necessary for the steel furnaces, as well as on all classes of supplies, such as fire clay blocks, piping, pipe fittings, belting, oils and a score of other items, all absolutely necessary for the operation of their plants. The great bulk of these items are produced in and supplied by Ontario. The Ontario iron and steel producers have a great advantage over Nova Scotia in their relative distributing positions. Those of eastern Canada, Sydney and New Glasgow, are at the extreme east, more than a thousand miles from Montreal-as a matter of fact, 1,065 miles-which city is the eastern gateway to the markets of Quebec and Ontario, where 90 per cent of Nova Scotia's iron and steel products must be sold. We have practically little or no market for our iron east of the city of Montreal; that is the gateway for the great consuming centres of this country. To reach that gateway we must compete there with the iron and steel products of Europe which, whether from the continent or from Great Britain, are brought across at practi-
The Budget-Mr. Cantley

cally ballast rates. Our friends from the west are interested in this matter. If cheap tonnage is to come to the port of Montreal to move their grain to European markets, that tonnage needs a certain amount of stiffening for crossing the Atlantic, particularly in bad weather. The result is that they are willing to carry, and do carry, heavy tonnage such as iron, steel and coal at practically ballast rates. They are quite content if they get a rate sufficient to pay for the loading and discharge of the cargo, because they save time, make better weather and avoid damage to their ships by having a larger amount of ballast than the ordinary water ballast usually carried.
We in Nova Scotia must compete with those ballast freight rates and other conditions, and what are they? We must remember that at Montreal, Nova Scotia coal and steel must meet the competition of continental and British material produced with much lower paid labour and having the added advantage of ocean freight based on practically ballast rates of 6 shillings, or $1.44 per ton as against full carload rates from Sydney of $6.94 to $7.39 per ton, or a carload rate to Toronto of $11.20, as against say $2.69 from Hamilton to Toronto. The fact is that the Hamilton steel plant is so situated that probably from 75 per cent to 90 per cent of its output can be sold, and actually is sold, within one or two hundred miles of its mills. It also has the advantage of direct water transport and canal navigation to Montreal and all the lake towns between.
I have here some figures showing the difference between the freight rates from Nova Scotia to Montreal and from Hamilton to Montreal. I am not going to take time to deal with all these figures, except to point out that the lowest freight rate we have to Montreal is over $6 per ton, while on the other hand for several months during the year Hamilton has been and still is able to ship material through the St. Lawrence canals to Montreal for about $1 per ton. We in the maritime provinces have paid our share of the cost of the shipping facilities on the St. Lawrence sj^stem between. Ontario and Quebec, yet we must pay six times the rate they pay in order to get to the Montreal market. Mj' further point is that the very great advantage given Ontario and Quebec through the refunding of the duty on coal, as provided by tariff items 1019, 1049, 1065 and 1066, is a most unfair provision of the tariff as it stands to-day. No good reason can be shown why the Ontario iron and steel plants should be

so favoured and even less in so far as the coking plant situated on the Lachine canal side at Montreal is concerned more especially in view of the duty of one dollar now imposed on imported coke. I believe it can be demonstrated that the plants could easily absorb a dollar per ton on the coal they use.
I am sorry the ex-Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) is not in his seat. In his address he said this was a rich man's budget, but the new automobile duties do not point that way. He pointed to the higher postage rate. Yes, we are back to three cent postage, but why? We are back because of a $6,000,000 deficit as a result of the administration of hon. members opposite. Is this a tax which is principally paid by the poor man? I say it is not. I venture to say that 99 per cent of the postal revenue of Canada is provided by the business men, the manufacturers and merchants. They are the ones who pay that tax. In the annual expenditure of the so-called poor man, the farmer, the artisan or the labourer, postage is practically a negligible item.
By the way of further criticism of the budget the financial critic of the opposition stated "We will find that four-fifths of the total taxation is paid by the ordinary people of the country." No doubt that is quite true, but it is equally true that four-fifths, or indeed ninety-nine per cent, of Canadians are ordinary people. I should like to point out also that corporation dividends drawn by foreigners now are taxable; family corporations are abolished, and from the larger incomes the state will take annually one-quarter of every dollar. If this is a rich man's budget, it is not evident on the face of it.
For years in this house attention has been directed to the flood of objectionable, trashy literature coming into Canada, principally from the United States. The proposals now before the house are calculated to greatly lessen the influx of that type of literature- if it can be described by that name-and I am sure the whole country will welcome this step.
Our western friends have been sorely hit by the lack of markets for their grain. 1 note with pleasure the very considerably increased movement of wheat during the past few months, and I also welcome and cordially approve of the proposal of the Prime Minister to readjust rail freights on western grain by a contribution of five cents per bushel on all wheat of this year's crop exported. Canada is a great dominion with varied problems and interests. No one portion can suffer without all portions suffering, and any assistance given the west will ultimately benefit

The Budget-Miss Macphail
the east. Our interests are mutual, and the prosperity of the west is our prosperity. Therefore I applaud the action taken by the government in this matter.
With a few words I shall conclude. As far as unemployment is concerned, unfortunately the world has not seen the end of it and probably will not see the end for some time. Recovery must be and will be slow, but the action of the government, both at the short session of last year and in the legislation now before the house, will go far to meet our needs, and before long Canada again will prosper and progress to a degree which will not be excelled by any country on earth.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In rising to make a few observations on the budget, one naturally would like to say something complimentary and kind to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett), and I feel I can say that I appreciate the difficulty of the present time. I appreciate too the ability of the Minister of Finance, who is also Prime Minister, and I admire his capacity for hard work, a prodigious amount of which was entailed in the preparing of the budget- a budget which the Ottawa Citizen has truly described as a tremendous barrage of figures. After one has recovered from the extreme exhaustion of the onslaught, and has had time to read it over, there are, of course, some things in the budget that are generally acceptable. I am sure that the five cents a bushel on western wheat, in so far as it is of any use to the western farmer, is welcomed by Canada pretty generally. I believe too that the house and the country approve of the increase in the income tax on corporations from 8 to 10 per cent, and the increased tax on private incomes, so far as it goes. Having said that, I feel that even the good will which I bear the Minister of Finance will allow me to go no further.
I do not think that our present condition is due to overproduction, as has been often claimed, but rather to a faulty monetary system which does not provide enough currency to carry the goods from him who produces to him who wishes to consume them. There are very many authorities who take the stand that we are not really suffering from overproduction. In this connection I wish to quote from a recent speech by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, who was held in such high regard in this house. I quote from the journal of the Canadian Bankers' Association, Mr. Meighen, referring to over-production, said:
If those who have too much wheat can exchange that wheat with those who have too much of something else, of oil, of gasoline, of
clothing: if people are in a position to do that, the world can use all the wheat there is to-day and more, and can use all the oil that is produced and more, and all the clothing that is produced and more.
If people were in the position to exchange what they have too much of for what somebody else has too much of, we would see that there was not too much of anything. The trouble is that they are not in a position so to exchange.
Were the facilities of exchange adequate, were the world's monetary system adequate to demands for exchange, then the three per cent increase* in the world's products from year to year would mean a three per cent elevation in the standard of living each year for the masses of mankind.
We live in a machine age that produces goods in greater quantities from year to year; and as Mr. Meighen intimates, the amount of gold does not increase as rapidly as the goods in circulation. The result is that we have too little currency and depressed prices; prices are lower than they really ought to be. Our currency, instead of being based on the needs of the people and the necessity for distributing the goods which the people produce, is based on what I believe is an outworn system-the gold standard. And this is the first of six reasons which I hope to give for opposing the budget. A budget which to-day has nothing to suggest in the way of a change in the present monetary system is certainly a budget that can be condemned as a poor one. I consider a change in the monetary system to be more needed than anything else. It is more fundamental than anything else, and the budget says absolutely nothing about it.
The League of Nations have realized the importance of this monetary question, for they have appointed a commission known as the Gold Delegation of the League of Nations, to examine into the adequacy of the world's gold supply as a basis for world currency and credits, and the likelihood of meeting world trade in the years to come. This commission is composed of the world's greatest economists, who have brought in an interim report on these questions. It would seem to me just about time that we began, as a government, a parliament and a people, to listen to the opinions of the world's best economists, not only on the monetary question but as well with respect to trade.
I wish to quote one sentence of what Harold Laski has to say regarding the monetary question. I am quoting from a little book called " Politics." At page 143 this writer says:
No single cause produces such chaos in the modern world as the right of the individual state to control its monetary policy.

The Budget-Miss Macphail
The monetary policies of the powerful nations of the world are, at least in some degree, of concern to us all, and I think it is quite time that as a parliament we realized the necessity of coming to some international agreement on this question. And because the budget does not deal with it at all, does not indicate the need of any study or change in that direction, but rather clings to the very system that has brought about the condition of distress from which we are now suffering: because of this, if for no other reason, I would oppose the budget now before us.
Nor does the budget deal with unemployment. It says nothing whatever about this question. Yet this was the one problem that was before the country last July. Certainly it was the question on which most attention was centred. Indeed, it was so important last year that a special session of parliament was called in September, when we voted $20,000,000 for direct and indirect relief, at the same time raising the tariff considerably-all in the name of the unemployed. It was an exceedingly important question last year; but this year not a word is said about it. The budget does not mention it at all, and yet the conditions, as the Minister of Finance knows, are very much worse today than they were last July. Unemployment is more widespread than it was at that time, and the distress of this winter will be very much greater than it was last winter. Yet no provision is made in the budget to take care of the unemployed. For that second reason I must oppose the budget.
It seems to me that the Minister of Finance, in relieving the great incomes from as heavy taxation as they have borne in the past, has committed a grave error indeed. I think it was an error in judgment, and in this regard he has run counter to the psychology of the people, which I do not believe he understands. I thought he understood it, but obviously he would not have made a mistake like this if he did. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that there is more bitterness in the country over that one item in the budget than over almost all its other defects put together. Even in the closing words of the right hon. gentleman, as he was bringing his budget speech to a conclusion, he appealed to parliament and to the people to bear our common burden equally. Yet at a time like this, when burdens cannot easily be borne, a greater weight is put upon the shoulders of the common people of Canada, while the very rich are relieved in great measure of the burden which they have carried until now. This, I say, is undoubtedly 
giving rise to very much bitterness in the country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The attempt should not have been made to balance this budget by means of additional taxation. The fact that our commodity price level has fallen so sharply means that private debts have been increased, in many cases having more than doubled. Private individuals are carrying upon their shoulders a weight which hardly can be borne, and to add to that burden a new weight would seem to be too much. By attempting to balance next year's budget by means of taxation the Minister of Finance is taking from the people money which they have borrowed with great difficulty and at high rates of interest. Most people are facing this coming year on borrowed money; that certainly applies as far as extra taxes are concerned. Surely it would have been easier for the government to borrow money as a government. The taxes will be paid with borrowed money anyway, and the government could have borrowed it at much lower rates of interest than the private individual. I am

afraid I would go farther than that and ask this question: Is there any real obstacle to prevent the government from issuing direct the required amount of $75,000,000 or $80,000,000, the amount of the deficit? I do not think there is any obstacle except custom and a sort of miind set. If the government could not go that far, they certainly should have borrowed money on the credit of the country at large and not ask the people of Canada to carry this new' burden. This seventy-five or eighty millions of dollars is being taken out of the already painfully limited purchasing power of the people. Although some of it will go back into circulation it is taking money from those who have the least and who would spend all in buying goods, and putting the money into the hands of those who, for the most part, have more money than they have needs. Because I do not believe it to be good business to balance the budget in this way, I am opposed to the budget.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would not the printing of more money be equivalent to borrowing from the people?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not think so. I think the printing of more money would really be putting more currency into circulation. This is very badly needed and it would have a slight effect on improving business and raising prices because there would be more money to divide among the commodities on the market. I did not expect the house to agree with me, so I am not disappointed at the hon. member's attitude.
My fifth objection is that the budget increases the tariff. One would have supposed that the people of Canada would know now, if they are ever to know, that an increased tariff does not cure unemployment and does not raise the prices of farm products. If the people do not know that by now, then they are hopeless. The tariff brought down last September, as well as the one contained in the present budget, has decreased and will decrease still further imports and to that extent decrease exports, because it is true that if we do not buy neither can we sell. I think the present budget brings this government within the range of the criticism of Sir George Paish. In discussing politicians and statesmen . of the world, he is reported in the Montreal Gazette of June 9 as having said in New York:
They have done everything in their power to hamper trade. They have increased tariffs, they have raised embargoes, they have created licences; in fact, they left nothing undone to hamper trade. I wish to compliment the politicians and statesmen of the world upon the success of their policy. They have left uothing undone to hamper the trade of the world and 22110-168
The Budget-Miss Macphail
bring ruin. They have succeeded, but it means the suicide of the world. I am not saying that of New York, but of my country and of every country. It is essential that people should realize the danger in which they are, the danger of the complete breakdown of trade bringing unparalleled distress. This is no mere trade depression, it is a catastrophe of the first moment.
Several speakers on the government side of the house have rather preened themselves on the accomplishments of the tariff in September last, through its having brought to Canada eighty-seven new industries. That is all very interesting, but what I should like to know is this: where are the customers to be found who are going to buy the products of those eighty-seven new factories? If we could not consume the products of the factories which we had, how are we going to absorb the products of eighty-seven more? I shall await with great interest the government's explanation. I fancy the Minister of Finance must be impressed by this last fact, because speaking last year in connection with one of the large oil companies, he said:
They have their business all over the world. I made it abundantly clear that we preferred a refinery in Canada to one in Oklahoma and they intimated their intention to avail themselves of the opportunity of constructing a refinery in this country; and I believe they will probably do so. But they would not do so if this item were not there.
I suppose the Prime Minister is referring to the protection which had been given. Further on, in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), the Prime Minister said:
I am advised that the refineries are able to meet 50 per cent more than the present demand.
Why have another? That is exactly how I feel about the factories. I feel that the factories, the machines of industrial production that we had, could have met not only our needs but much more, if we could have consumed the goods rapidly enough to allow them to work at full steam. Therefore I really do not take seriously this gain that is supposed to have come from the tariff of last September. I often wonder how the Canadian manufacturer-I mean the really Canadian manufacturer, if such an animal can be run to ground anywhere-feels when these factories which the higher tariffs have induced to come, arrive backed by the great wealth of their country, and are his competitors within his own field. I often wonder whether he is as happy about the matter as we are led to suppose. With the radio, you know, I have had such a dose of Campbell's soup, it makes me wonder. I just cannot imagine the other

The bearer, the wealthy holders of such bonds, will have the privilege of pocketing their interest without paying the income tax, while revenues will be collected from the masses by means of heavy taxes.

The Budget-Mr. Raymond
The Conservative party had censured butter importation under the Liberal rule as ruinous to the dairy industry and as being the real cause of the slump in prices. When in office, not only did it not bar Australian butter imports, but it favoured them by ceasing to apply the dumping duty of 6 cents per pound; thus reducing the duty from 7 cents to 1 cent, and facilitating the importation of some million pounds of Australian butter since October last.
Moreover, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) had come to an understanding with Australia that not a pound of butter should be sold on the Canadian market at a price less than 32 cents. The agreement stood as long as the price of butter remained above 32 cents, but the day it fell below 32 cents, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) was prone to relieve Australia of this agreement, allowing the latter to flood the market with 750,000 pounds of butter

this lowered the price of our own by 10 to 12 cents per pound.
Why? His answer was that it was through courtesy to a sister nation. Is that fostering the policy of "Canada first?"
The speech from the throne had promised us measures which were to shower upon us unheard prosperity. What do we find in this budget? Taxation.
While the workman is out of work, the farmer sees the price of his products dwindling down from day to day reaching below the cost of production, new taxes are piled on him: 4 cents a pound on tea, 4 per cent on all articles purchased, etc. In the meantime, those who are in a better position to pay, those who have an income of more than $25,000 per year, see their taxes decreased. The rich are relieved in order to burden the poor.
Another measure brought down to remedy the present situation is tariff increase. The protection requested by manufacturers is directed against cheaper products, in order to boost the price of their goods. It is certainly not by examining the balance sheets of large companies that one shall find justification for this measure. Glance over the figures of the income tax of last year, $73,000,000. The income tax returns have increased by a few million dollars each year, although the income tax rate has decreased.
It was contended that high tariff would bring more work to the workman and better wages. The history of protection teaches us that this regime never contributed to obtaining more work or better wages for the working class but simply increased the cost of living and the profits of capitalists. I shall give you an instance. Take the case of textiles in industry.
'Air. Raymond.]
Every one knows that within the last few years, owing to fashion changes and the competition of artificial silk, the textile industry is passing through a world wide crisis. Nevertheless, dividends paid by textile companies in Canada have increased 11J per cent in 1928 as compared with the average dividend paid from 1922 to 1926.
Briefly, this is the history of the Dominion Textile Co., which produces more than all the other companies of its kind. It was organized in 1905 by the merging of a number of companies operating cotton factories in various localities.
Over and above the bonds bearing interest and the preferred stock on which a fixed dividend of 7 per cent has always regularly been paid, the company issued in favour of the original stock-holders 50,000 common shares at S10 per share, that is $500,000 worth.
The very first year, it paid on this common stock a dividend of $6 per share, or the equivalent of 60 per cent on this investment. The dividend was increased from year to year up to 1922, when it had reached $12 per share, which represented 120 per cent on the original investment.
You will recall that in 1919, at the inquiry on the cost of living, the general manager of the Dominion Textile Co. admitted that in 1918, the company had realized 291 per cent net profits. In 1922, its shareholders were again given the privilege of subscribing to 25,000 additional shares at S100 per share, and on which a $12 dividend per share was paid. The same year, fearing that a dividend of $12 per share might rouse the public, a new company was organized under the same name and every common stockholder received three shares for one, with a dividend of $4 or the equivalent of $12 on the old shares. In 1924 the dividend was increased to $5 per share or the equivalent of $15 on the old shares and the equivalent of 150 per cent on the initial investment of 8500,000. From 1924 up to this date, the company has paid, without interruption, dividends which are equivalent to 150 per cent on the initial investment of $500,000, and 15 per cent on the second subcription of $2,500,000 made in 1922.
In February 1928, following an inquiry before the Tariff Board, where producers and consumers were heard, the Liberal Government made some tariff reductions on cotton goods. The general manager of the Dominion Textile Co., the same person who appeared before the Board of Inquiry on the cost of living and who had admitted that in 1918, his company had made 291 per cent, protested. He even wrote to the hon. Minister of

speechtext:
What are we to think of those, whose age has lowered the intensive yield, that modern methods of industry call for,-who are thanked for their services and left absolutely without resources.
Is the worker not entitled to a fair share of the results of his labour just like the capitalist is entitled to a reasonable return for his investment?
When the Montreal Cottons Co. was realizing excessive profits, thanks to tariff protection which it deemed indispensable to exist, but which, in truth, only served to increase the price of its goods to the consumer, and thus increase its profits, it never gave to the workman that part of the wages to which he was entitled and which to-day would shelter him from want.
No day passes that I have not to listen to the sad complaints of these good people, whose distress is all the more worthy of being looked after, because unemployment to which they fall victim seems to be the reckoning of the new methods of overproduction, brought on by over-capitalization, and fostered by high tariff.
Poverty knocks at the door of too many artisans' home. And what does the gover-ment do? It increases the tariff on textile products, when the balance sheets of companies are before them, showing outrageous profits; and when these companies in order to increase production and their profits, replace hand-labour by machinery, overloading the worker who remains, while lowering his wages already insufficient. Is this protection for the workman? The problem of unemployment will not be solved by increasing production and decreasing the number of wage earners. The government does not stop at this. It reduces the rich man's taxes to place them on the workman with decreased wages or on the unemployed, by taxing all articles of first necessity, and it cries out to him: "have courage and confidence."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to offer a few observations I do so as the representative of a constituency of western Canada, a constituency whose people are ninety-five per cent dependent upon agriculture for a livelihood. Since the presentation of the budget I have received many letters from my constituents offering congratulations, appreciation and thanks to the government for the attention that they have given agriculture by the budget and by their general policy, and I have been asked to convey those sentiments to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett).
*At the outset, Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make on behalf of the farmer of western Canada. It seems to me that those hon. members of the east and of the extreme west who do not know the farmer of western Canada personally will, if they have formed their impressions from speeches emanating from western members of the other side of the house, reach an entirely erroneous conclusion of what kind of man the western farmer is. I am afraid that if they accept those speeches at their face value they will picture the farmer as a selfish, grasping, whining, dissatisfied sort of fellow. This is very, very far from the truth. I think it was the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) who the other day hit the nail on the head when he referred to the western farmer as the "king of optimists." He is an optimist. He has a lot to contend with, but he is not a quitter, and he is prepared to expend all the energy he possesses to make a success of the work in which he is engaged. He is out there to-day with his back to the wall putting up a magnificent fight. He asks quarter from no man, but he does expect justice and fair play. Accorded these, you can depend upon it that the western farmer will make his full contribution to the upbuilding and development of this great dominion of ours, and will do his full share towards stabilizing the economic conditions as they exist to-day.
There is something else to be said about the western farmer. He is not jealous of the east. Perhaps, judging from the speeches to which I have referred, easterners may think that he is. Let me assure the house that there is no member of any section of the population of this country who will be more ready to rejoice at every indication of returning prosperity and improved conditions in eastern Canada than the western farmer. He will rejoice for two reasons; first, he is a true Canadian, interested in the welfare of Canada as a whole; secondly, he fully realizes that almost immediately those improved conditions
2fi48
The Budget-Mr. Burns

will be reflected in better times in western Canada.
The western farmer is a firm believer in the Conservative policy of "Canada first." Notwithstanding what the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien) said when addressing the house last week, we did preach that policy throughout the length and breadth of Manitoba during the last election. That policy the farmers of Manitoba accepted when they returned to this house a large representation pledged to the Conservative cause. If proof of the statement is required that the western farmer is a believer in the Conservative policy of Canada first, I would refer hon. members to the results of the election of July last, when the province returned to this house one Liberal, one National Progressive, two Liberal Progressives, two members of the Labour group, and eleven Conservatives.
The hon. member for Provencher, in answer to a question from this side of the house, said that he hoped the Prime Minister was not trying to convert the farmers of western Canada to the policy of protection by offering them the five cent subvention on wheat. It seems to me this is indicative of a feeling of alarm in the mind of the hon. member. I can say to him now, and give him fair warning, that he has cause for alarm as to the trend of the thoughts of the farmers of western Canada in this respect. We as a Conservative party are rapidly gaining the support and confidence of that section of our people. In the federal election of 1925 there were 43,700 votes registered in support of Conservative candidates in the rural portion of Manitoba. During the election of 1926 that number increased to something over 56,000, while in 1930 the rural vote in Manitoba in favour of Conservative candidates was over 76,000. I think this shows that the farmer is turning to the Conservative party and Conservative policies to lead him out of the rather difficult situation in which he has found himself during the last few years.
The other evening the hon. member for Provencher, discussing the effect of the tariff upon the cost of goods to the consumer, dealt with the matter of agricultural implements.
He chose a rather isolated case and quoted prices from some catalogue of which I had never before heard, to show that a pickling machine for the treatment of grain for smut had increased in cost over the catalogue price quoted by the same company in 1930. I know nothing of that firm or of the line of goods to which he referred, but I can direct the hon. member to a manufacturing concern in my home city of Portage la Prairie which will sell him a pickling machine to-day for less money than he would have paid for it if bought from the same firm in 1930.
As I listened to the remarks of the hon. member in reference to that catalogue, I wondered why he did not analyse the price lists of the leading agricultural implement firms of this country in order to show the effect of the tariff upon the prices of goods. When I went home, however, and procured those catalogues myself and examined them, the answer was obvious. They do nothing at all to prove the contention of my hon. friend. For purposes of record, and to combat the argument put forward by the hon. member for Provencher, I have analysed the figures contained in the catalogues of four large implement concerns of Canada. So far as western Canada is concerned, I would say that these four firms sell at least ninety per cent of the implements used in that portion of the country.' I refer to the Massey Harris Company, the International Harvester Company, the Cockshutt Plow Company and the John Deere Company. I wish to tell you, Mr. Speaker, just what that analysis shows. That is what we told the farmers in Manitoba, at any rate in the constituency of Portage la Prairie, and I can go back to them and tell them that policy was carried out and that they have been protected.
The hon. member for Provencher, in the course of his remarks the other night, said:
If the hon. members for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), Souris (Mr. Willis), Selkirk (Mr. Stitt), Portage la Prairie (Mr. Burns),
[Mr. Burns.)
Dauphin (Mr. Bowman), Nelson (Mr. Stitt), Springfield (Mr. Hay), and Brandon (Mr. Beaubier) had told their electors that if the present Prime Minister was returned to power he would increase the tariff, I do not believe they would be here to-day. They know that very well, and they know that they told the electors that the Conservative party was not a high tariff party. Can they go back to their electors to-day and tell them that? If they do they will be misleading those who put them in office.
I do not know how the hon. member know3 what we told the people in the constituency of Portage la Prairie. So far as I am aware, he never entered that constituency during the contest. I feel absolutely sure that the information was not given him by my Liberal opponent in the last election. I am proud to acknowledge my Liberal opponent as one of the closest personal friends I have in the world, and I can say that in that contest, on both sides, there was a clean fight. I do not believe there was any cleaner contest anywhere throughout the dominion, and I think Mr. McPherson will tell the hon. member that we did not go about our constituency making misrepresentations to the electors during the campaign.
As regards the farmers of western Canada, we might ask ourselves this question: What are they interested in to-day? It seems to me they are interested in the prices of agricultural implements, in wheat, barley, eggs, butter and farm produce, and in live stock. And what has been the effect of the Conservative policy upon these things in which the farmer of the west is interested?
First we come to the matter of agricultural implements. I believe the statement was made from the opposite side the other night that the policy of the Conservative party was reflected in the prices of agricultural implements. Now I have shown that the only change which has taken place since 1930 has been a reduction, and therefore I say that if it is true that the Conservative policy is reflected in the prices of agricultural implements the farmers of Canada will say, "Give us more Conservative policy."
I have no brief for the manufacturers of agricultural implements. I have a feeling, in common with many of the people of the west, that the prices of these implements are too high. Those figures I have given to-night were quoted simply to show the effect of the tariff on the prices of agricultural implements, and for no other purpose. So far as the prices of these implements are concerned, I should like to see the government take some action for an investigation. I do not know whether the prices are too high or not. If an investigation is held, witnesses summoned to

The Budget-Mr. Burns
give evidence and the manufacturers of implements can prove to the people that their prices are fair and square, it would be to their advantage and put them in better odour with the farmers of western Canada. If, on the other hand, it is found that these prices are not fair, that they are too high, I would say that no time should be lost in taking whatever steps are necessary to secure lower prices on agricultural implements for the farmers of this country.
The farmer is interested in wheat. What has been the effect upon this commodity of the action taken by the government? First, we have the five cent subvention, at which hon. members on the other side of the house would like to laugh. I can assure them that the farmer is not laughing at this action. It has been referred to by some hon. members as the second five cent speech. I wonder who made the first? The farmer of western Canada does not look upon this as a five cent speech but, based upon a conservative estimate of the amount of grain upon which that five cent subvention will apply, it is looked upon as a ten million dollar speech. There is a large surplus of wheat in store in this country for which markets must be found. Has this government done anything to find markets for that surplus wheat? The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) told the house the other night of the efforts made at the Imperial conference to find and encourage markets for Canadian wheat. He told us that they found a feeling existing in England that the grain exporters of Canada were taking or trying to take an unfair advantage of the European countries, that Canadians were trying to corner the wheat markets so that they could dictate the prices. As the hon. minister said, we do not for one moment agree that there was any thought of that nature in the minds of the grain people of Canada, but yet that feeling existed. He told the house of the steps taken to disabuse the minds of the people of Europe of that fact, and I believe, and I think we all believe, that the efforts made in that respect bore fruit. The hon. minister told us that in visiting the continent he found that in Holland, Belgium, France, Germany and Denmark the millers were changing their silk screens in order to make them serviceable for the milling of Argentine wheat. They talked to these people and did what they could to combat this movement. They must have been more or less successful because we find that every one of the countries named have increased their purchases of wheat from Canada in 1931 over their purchases in 1930.
We have been told that the trade commissioners of this country stationed throughout the world have been asked to concentrate upon the finding of markets for Canadian wheat. Not only does this apply to the trade commissioners at present functioning, but additional junior trade commissioners have been appointed and have been sent out into the world with the same instructions-find us an outlet for the surplus wheat of this country.
This government has shown in many ways that it is interested in agricultural matters and that it is doing its utmost to help solve the present problems. I think the results which follow must be attributed to the efforts made by the government. We were told the other day that in 1929-30 the exports of wheat from this country amounted to 155,000,000 bushels; for the first ten months of 1930-31 they amounted to 195,000,000 bushels, and a conservative estimate based upon information as to the bookings for June and July will bring that total up to 234,000,000 bushels for the year, an increase over 1929-30 of 79,000,000 bushels. This is something that interests the farmer of western Canada. When I refer to western Canada I do not intend to limit my remarks to that part of the country. It is the part familiar to me, but we do not claim to have a monopoly on the word "farmer". Perhaps it would be better to substitute the words "farmers of Canada" for the words "western Canada."
This government took very generous action last spring in the way of seed grain relief. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) told us the other day that this offer was more generous than that ever before made by any federal government, because of the arrangement made with the premiers of the western provinces, the terms of the agreement cannot be divulged at the present time, but the minister told the house that when these terms are made known the people of Canada as a whole will be well satisfied with the generous assistance which has been rendered.
There is another thing which reflects the feeling of the Minister of Agriculture, another thing which shows his interest in the producer of agricultural products. Those hon. members who were present the other morning at the meeting of the select standing committee on agriculture will remember the opening words of the minister. He said that he would like the committee to inquire into ways and means of getting into the hands of the producer more of the money actually realized in the sale of wheat. Is that not a laudable objective? He told the committee that he was not relying upon it, entirely, to formulate his policy, that

The Budget-Mr. Bums
he had his policy framed, and that he had his own fixed ideas in the matter, but that he was always ready to receive suggestions which would help him to market the wheat of Canada to the advantage of the producers in Canada.
The farmer is interested in butter and eggs, and I think the action taken by this government in this respect is acceptable to the people of western Canada. During the elections of July last we Conservative members did not have to talk much protection, we found the farmer doing most of the talking along that line. He was insistent that his products should be protected from the flood of dairy products from other lands. The action taken by this government in shutting out those imports from other countries is what the farmer asked for, and that is what he has received. The action in putting an eight-cent duty upon butter and in coming to an arrangement with Australia stands to the credit of this government. The old agreement was still in force under which it was permissible to send butter from Australia into this country under a one-cent duty, but the government made a verbal arrangement with the officials of Australia whereby they were not to release butter to this country under thirty-two cents per pound without first receiving consent. That shows that this government has a thought for the dairy farmer, and it shows action in the right direction.
Let us look for a moment at the results obtained because of the action taken by this government. I have the figures under my hand, and I am going to deal with just three months of 1930 and three months of 1931.
